Reviewed routing, explicit selection, evals, review panels, and smoke checks. Targeted tests could not complete because the installed dependencies lack zod's overwrite method and the MCP SDK client module; the origin-specific router tests passed.

findings.title: Return a declined answer when exclusions exhaust the route
findings.detail: The last-resort return happens before exclusion reasons are inspected. An invocation can therefore succeed with a previously declined answer even though the only remaining candidate was excluded, rather than failing with the required origin reason.
findings.suggestion: Handle origin-exhausted decisions before returning a last-resort answer, and cover a declined allowed model followed by an excluded fallback.
findings.failure_scenario: An allowed decision model declines with lastResort set, and the only untried fallback has an excluded origin. The invocation returns the declined answer instead of failing with origin excluded.

findings.title: Preserve exclusion reasons when remaining verifiers are ineligible
findings.detail: Exclusion reasons are reported only when every listed verifier was filtered by origin. If an allowed verifier remains but shares a checkpoint with a finder, pickVerifier throws its own error and discards the excluded verifier's reason. The operator cannot see why the independent verifier was unavailable.
findings.suggestion: Include collected exclusion reasons when verifier selection fails after filtering.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier list contains an allowed model that raised the candidate and an independent CN-origin model excluded by configuration. Selection fails with only the allowed model's checkpoint error and omits origin excluded.

findings.title: Skip native smoke checks when all of their models are excluded
findings.detail: Native smoke checks still run when every model for a native provider is excluded. cheapestModel throws the exclusion reason, which the smoke runner records as a failure. Consequently, deploy --smoke fails even when other eligible providers are available. Backend checks already treat this condition as a skip.
findings.suggestion: Mark native provider checks skipped when that provider has catalog models but none are origin-eligible.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure exclude_origins to exclude all Claude models while Codex or another provider remains eligible, then run deployment with --smoke: each Claude check fails with an origin-excluded error and the smoke gate fails.

findings.title: Preserve exclusion reasons when no independent verifier remains
findings.detail: The exclusion reason is included only when every listed verifier is excluded. If an allowed verifier remains in the list but its checkpoint raised the finding, pickVerifier rejects it and reports only that the remaining verifier raised a candidate. The excluded independent verifier and its required skip reason disappear from the failure.
findings.suggestion: Include collected exclusion reasons when verifier selection fails because the remaining eligible targets cannot independently verify the batch.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier roster contains an allowed model that raised the finding and an independent CN-origin model excluded by configuration. Verification fails without the origin-excluded reason even though the exclusion removed the only usable verifier.

Reviewed routing, explicit model validation, runtime catalog updates, evals, and visibility. Focused router tests covering exclusions passed. The broader targeted command could not complete because the installed Zod lacks number().overwrite; eval and HTTP tests failed to load for that environment dependency mismatch.

findings.title: An excluded verifier aborts an eval even when another verifier is eligible
findings.detail: The evaluation runner converts every configured verifier to a target before selecting one. `router.toTarget` now throws for an excluded origin, so one excluded member aborts preparation of the entire trial instead of allowing `pickVerifier` to select an eligible alternative. This can occur when a runtime catalog model is changed while an evaluation is queued; production verifier selection filters excluded alternatives first.
findings.suggestion: Filter excluded verifier alternatives before constructing targets, preserving their reasons for the no-eligible-verifier case.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval panel has verifier targets A and B, both eligible at submission. Before a queued trial prepares, A is patched to an excluded origin while B remains eligible. Preparing the verifier list throws on A and the trial fails without trying B.

findings.title: Filtered verifier exclusions are absent from the run log
findings.detail: Verifier targets removed by the new filtering are kept only in a local array. When another verifier remains, those reasons are discarded and the router sees only the selected target, so its logged skip list cannot contain the excluded verifier. If the remaining targets all raised the finding, `pickVerifier` also fails without mentioning the excluded alternative.
findings.suggestion: Record the excluded verifier reasons in the run log and include them when no usable verifier remains.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel has a CN-origin verifier and an allowed verifier. The allowed verifier is selected, but the run log contains no `origin excluded (CN; baseOrigin=CN)` reason for the skipped verifier.

findings.title: Executable text is still blocked when it is not strict UTF-8

findings.detail: The new mode guard requires strict UTF-8 and rejects several control bytes, although the request says executable text should be treated like other text. findings.detail: The new mode check applies to every path whose bytes fail reviewableText, rather than only to paths matching INERT_MEDIA_PATH. Git treats NUL-free files as text, but reviewableText rejects escape characters and invalid UTF-8. As a result, ordinary executable scripts can still be reported as binary-content despite having a readable Git diff, contrary to the requested fix.

findings.title: The interruption check still relies on a fixed scheduling window
findings.detail: After releasing the gate, the test waits 800 ms before checking the log. If stop returns while leaving the check alive but the check is not scheduled during that window, the assertion can pass even though the check will later write "end". This leaves the added verification dependent on runner scheduling.
findings.suggestion: Use an observable process-completion or cancellation signal to establish that the original check has terminated before asserting its log, rather than relying on a fixed delay.

findings.title: Recheck deferred triggers against the observed head even when the poller head is unchanged
findings.detail: The outer condition compares the new head with the poller's previous snapshot, while the database predicate compares it with each trigger's observed head. findings.title: A stale snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: Any saved poller snapshot is treated as authoritative, even if it predates the land queue's observation. If its head differs from the approved head, startConflictTrigger marks the durable trigger skipped. No subsequent land-queue processing retries that trigger, so the blocked entry can remain unresolved. A saved snapshot can likewise be stale about draft or open state.
findings.suggestion: Obtain a current PR observation before consuming a land trigger, and retain the trigger pending when its eligibility cannot be established.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last saved head A; the PR advances to head B and is approved; the land queue detects a conflict at B before the next poll. The saved A snapshot causes the B trigger to be marked skipped.

findings.title: Conflict rows consume the previous release's review-round limit
findings.detail: The migration stores conflict rounds in the existing review_rounds table. The previous release reads every row as a review round and counts all of them toward its review cap. After rollback, conflict rounds can therefore cause an ordinary review request to put the owner into needs_human instead of creating its review round. This violates the requirement that the previous release remain usable after a deploy rollback.
findings.suggestion: Keep conflict-round records invisible to the previous release's review-round counting, using a rollback-compatible representation.
findings.failure_scenario: A new release creates conflict rounds for a PR, then the deployment rolls back. A later changes-requested review is handled by the old release, which counts those conflict rows against its review cap and refuses the review round.

findings.title: The PR comment does not summarize the resolution
findings.detail: The comment reports the merged base, conflicted file names, and resulting SHA, but does not say how the conflicting changes were resolved. A reviewer cannot learn the resolution from the required PR comment.
findings.suggestion: Include a concise summary of the actual resolution in the comment, using information produced and checked during the round.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict changes behavior in a file; the delivered PR comment lists that file and the merge SHA but gives no description of the chosen behavior.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot permanently discards a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: When any saved snapshot exists, trigger processing uses it without refreshing the PR. `startConflictTrigger` marks a head mismatch as skipped, so an ordinary delay between a new head being approved and the next poll can permanently discard the landing queue's trigger.
findings.suggestion: Refresh or defer the trigger when the saved observation does not match the blocked entry's head; do not consume it based on stale state.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last recorded head A, a user approves newer head B, and the landing queue detects that B conflicts with the base before the next poll. The trigger for B is marked `PR head moved` using the saved A snapshot, and no conflict round starts when B is subsequently observed.

findings.title: Transient PR lookup failures can leave a durable trigger pending indefinitely
findings.detail: A failed lookup leaves the trigger pending, but the landing queue only processes pending triggers at startup and after another entry blocks. If this PR is not tracked by the poller and no further entry blocks, recovery from a transient GitHub failure does not start the round until another daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Schedule bounded reprocessing of pending triggers while the service is running, including triggers for PRs without a saved poller snapshot.
findings.failure_scenario: A landing conflict records a trigger for a PR without a saved snapshot. The immediate `gh pr view` fails transiently, then GitHub recovers. With no subsequent queue block or restart, the trigger remains pending and the conflict round never starts.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before validating the PR head
findings.detail: Delivery mutates the PR's auto-merge setting before checking the current remote head and the stored authorization. If the PR head or round authorization changed while the resolution ran, delivery correctly refuses the push afterwards but has already disabled auto-merge on the changed PR.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current PR identity, head, and round authorization before changing auto-merge, and revalidate after asynchronous operations as needed.
findings.failure_scenario: A human pushes a new PR head and enables auto-merge while a conflict round is running. The round reaches delivery, disables auto-merge, then rejects the push because the head no longer matches the reviewed SHA.

findings.title: Restored results skip setup after the checkout is cleaned
findings.detail: After a restart, the gates stage calls checkoutCommitted, which removes ignored build products and dependencies, before this function returns the saved initial result. A pending local regression retry then runs without the setup and build output produced by the initial execution. The baseline resume path likewise cleans the worktree before reusing the saved baseline result. This changes retry outcomes and can turn a flaky check into a blocking failure or hide a regression in the baseline.
findings.suggestion: Ensure local retries resumed after a restart have the setup and working-tree state they require, or replay the relevant local execution before retrying.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate setup installs dependencies, the initial check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts after saving that result or starting its retry. On resume, checkoutCommitted removes the dependencies; the saved result bypasses setup and the retry fails because its executable is missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: executeGate awaits only execution.result and never reads execution.events. Local execution happens to emit existing gate notifications through a separate hook, but an executor implementing the interface has no access to that hook. Its check events therefore never reach the run event stream or landing log. An executor whose event producer requires its stream to be drained can also leave result pending indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream and forward its events to the appropriate gate reporting hooks, coordinating stream completion and errors with the result.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor emits a check event and then returns a GateRun. The stage completes, but the check event is absent from the run's gate events and the landing log.

findings.title: Cached initial results skip rebuilding the worktree before a resumed retry
findings.detail: After a restart, the stage returns the saved initial GateRun without rerunning its setup or checks. Both prepare and the gates stage clean the worktree before reaching this point, so a pending baseline or regression retry runs without files produced by the initial attempt. Previously, resuming the stage reran the initial gates and recreated those files before retrying. This can change the retry verdict and baseline cache contents.
findings.suggestion: Preserve or reconstruct the initial execution's required worktree state before resuming a local retry, and test a restart with a retry that depends on generated build output.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command creates an untracked build artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts before its retry completes. Resume cleans the artifact, reuses the saved initial result, and the retry fails because the artifact is missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: The shared execution path awaits only `execution.result` and never reads `execution.events`. Local execution happens to call the legacy hooks directly, but an injected executor can report progress and check results only through its event stream. Those events never reach pipeline gate events or the landing log, so the interface does not preserve the existing observable behavior for executors using the advertised seam.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream while awaiting the result and route its events through the existing pipeline and landing reporting paths. Cover this with an executor that emits events without invoking local hooks.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor emits a failed check event and then returns its GateRun. The stage verdict reflects the result, but the run has no per-check gate event and the landing log contains no check output.

findings.detail: The persisted local handle contains the request used by `attach` to replay work, but `redactGateData` rewrites every string in that request. Registered credential values are replaced and terminal control characters are stripped from paths, check names and commands. A resumed local execution can therefore run different commands or fail to find its working directory. The same transformation of results also changes command strings used to match retry candidates.
findings.suggestion: Persist an opaque local handle and reconstruct its request from trusted run state on resume, without storing or modifying secret-bearing execution inputs.

findings.title: Restore the first attempt's workspace before replaying a retry
findings.detail: Completed attempts are reused after restart, but prepare and gates clean the worktree before reaching this code. A pending local retry then runs without the generated files left by its first attempt, even though retries previously ran before cleanup specifically to preserve that build output. This can change a retry verdict and consequently hide or report a regression incorrectly.
findings.suggestion: For local executions, replay the preceding attempt when its workspace effects are no longer available, or durably preserve and restore the required workspace before attaching the retry.
findings.failure_scenario: A first check generates an untracked build artifact and fails transiently; the daemon restarts after starting its retry. Resume cleans the artifact, reuses the saved first result, and runs the retry against a different workspace.

findings.detail: `executeGate` awaits only `execution.result` and never reads `execution.events`. Local execution happens to call the supplied hooks directly, but an injected executor has no access to those hooks. Its check events therefore never reach pipeline gate events or the landing log, and an executor whose event stream requires consumption can stall.

output.summary:
Reviewed the gate and editor read policies and ran targeted sandbox tests. Real Seatbelt probes could not run inside the existing confinement; some unit tests also encountered this review environment’s denied home paths.

The gate policy leaves Cargo registry credentials readable through its toolchain allowance. I checked the generated policy and ran focused tests. Real Seatbelt probes were skipped because nested Seatbelt is unavailable in this sandbox; other test failures were caused by denied access to host paths and an incompatible installed Zod dependency.

findings.title: Cargo credential files remain readable to gate commands
findings.detail: The gate policy allows reads throughout CARGO_HOME, but the denied credential list does not include Cargo’s credentials files. The generated profile therefore allows ~/.cargo/credentials and ~/.cargo/credentials.toml, which can contain registry tokens. Candidate tests or dependency scripts can read and exfiltrate those tokens. This conflicts with the requirement that credential stores fall outside the gate allowlist.
findings.suggestion: Deny Cargo credential files explicitly after the toolchain allowance, while preserving the reads needed by Cargo, and add a real Seatbelt probe using a temporary stand-in credential file.
findings.failure_scenario: A user has a registry token in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml and runs a gate against a malicious dependency; the dependency reads that file by absolute path and sends the token over HTTPS.

findings.title: Cargo home allowance exposes registry credentials to gates
findings.detail: The gate profile allows the entire Cargo home, but the credential deny list does not include Cargo's credentials files. Candidate gate code can therefore read registry tokens from the default ~/.cargo/credentials.toml or legacy ~/.cargo/credentials and send them over the unrestricted network. A targeted policy check, `bun -e 'import { homeReadPolicy, readPolicyScope } from "./src/harness/read-policy.ts"; const home = process.env.TMPDIR!; readPolicyScope.run({home}, () => { const p = homeReadPolicy([home + "/work"], true); console.log(JSON.stringify({cargoAllowed: p.allowRead?.includes(home + "/.cargo"), cargoCredentialsDenied: p.denyRead.includes(home + "/.cargo/credentials.toml")})); });'`, printed `{"cargoAllowed":true,"cargoCredentialsDenied":false}`.
findings.suggestion: Keep the required Cargo toolchain paths readable while explicitly denying Cargo credential files, including under a configured CARGO_HOME, and add a probe for them.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner has a registry token in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml and a malicious dependency or test runs as a gate command.

findings.title: Retry executions are discarded instead of reattached after restart
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial and rebase handles qualify for reattachment. A persisted baseline-retry, timeout or regression-retry handle is cleared on resume, and the stage starts work again. For an executor whose work survives daemon restarts, the original execution can continue independently while a duplicate runs; its result is never consumed. The new test explicitly expects this behavior for retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough prior stage state to resume each retry and attach to its stored handle, rather than discarding it.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after starting a remote regression retry but before receiving its result. On resume it starts the initial gates again and eventually launches another retry, while the original retry remains running.

findings.title: An attach error clears the durable handle for work that may still be running
findings.detail: A synchronous attach failure calls onSettled even though no execution result was obtained. The caller consequently deletes the persisted handle. An attach failure does not establish that the underlying execution ended, so a subsequent stage attempt cannot reconnect to it and may start duplicate work.
findings.suggestion: Keep the handle durable when attach fails, and clear it only after the execution has actually settled or its cancellation has been confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor starts a job and persists its handle, but attach throws because its connection is temporarily unavailable. The handle is deleted while the job continues, and a subsequent attempt starts another job.

findings.title: Restart discards handles for in-flight retries
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A persisted timeout, baseline-retry, or regression-retry handle is discarded on resume, and the stage starts new work. After a process restart, cancelGateExecution cannot cancel the old execution because its live execution map is process-local. This violates the requested restart contract and can leave the original execution running alongside its replacement. The new restart test explicitly expects this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough preceding stage state to resume each retry and attach to its stored handle without starting a replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after a regression retry has started and its handle has been saved but before its result is recorded. On resume, the saved retry handle is cleared and new gate executions are started.

findings.title: Landing executions have no durable handle
findings.detail: The landing queue calls executeGate without a persistence callback or stored handle, so its handle exists only in memory. If the daemon restarts while landing checks are running, the queue cannot reattach to that execution and instead starts the checks again. A durable executor may continue running the original checks after the daemon exits.
findings.suggestion: Persist the landing execution handle with the queue entry and restore it when checks resume, clearing it only when the result is durably recorded.
findings.failure_scenario: A landing check is started by an executor whose work survives daemon restart; the daemon restarts before the queue records completion, and the resumed queue starts a second execution.

findings.title: Retry executions are discarded instead of reattached after restart

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a remote regression retry is running; on resume it discards that retry's handle and starts another execution while the original continues.

findings.title: Handle is cleared before the result is durably recorded
findings.detail: The finally block saves state with the handle removed before the caller records the baseline or gate comparison. A crash after this save but before the caller's checkpoint loses both the result and its execution identity. Resume therefore starts the work again instead of attaching to the completed execution.
findings.suggestion: Keep the handle until the corresponding result and stage progress are saved together, or persist the result before clearing it.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate execution completes and `gate-result` is saved, then the daemon stops before `lastGates` or the baseline is saved. On restart there is no handle to attach and the executor starts another gate run.

findings.title: Landing executions have no durable handle
findings.detail: Landing calls `executeGate` without a persistence callback or stored handle, so its default callback discards the execution identity. A restart during landing checks cannot reattach to work that survives the daemon and instead starts another execution.
findings.suggestion: Persist the landing check handle with the landing entry and restore it on resume before starting new work.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a landing check is running on a durable executor; the resumed queue starts another check and leaves the original execution untracked.

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after a regression retry has started but before its result is consumed. On restart, the pending retry handle is discarded and the pipeline starts the initial gates and retry again.

findings.title: Handle is cleared before the result is durably incorporated

Reviewed the preview confinement and process lifecycle. The targeted preview suite could not exercise its server paths: this sandbox denied loopback listening with EPERM, and the real Seatbelt test was skipped because nested Seatbelt is unavailable.

findings.title: Preview output without newlines can exhaust daemon memory
findings.detail: The new serve path uses runConfined, which installs line callbacks through runProcess. Its lineSplitter accumulates all output until a newline without applying tailLimit. A candidate server can therefore emit an arbitrarily long line while remaining alive, causing unbounded memory growth in the factory daemon. The previous serve implementation bounded its collected output to 4,000 characters. Build and seed also pass through runSandboxed's stdout line callback and have the same exposure until they exit.
findings.suggestion: Bound the line splitter's pending buffer or use a bounded raw-chunk callback for preview output while preserving startup detection.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview serve command repeatedly writes bytes to stdout without a newline while serving requests; the daemon retains the growing line until it exhausts memory.

findings.title: Cancellation can leave an unhandled shutdown rejection
findings.detail: The abort listener discards the promise returned by stop(). The new stop implementation deliberately rethrows ProcessTerminationError when process shutdown cannot be confirmed, so cancellation after the preview has been returned can produce an unhandled rejection in the daemon. This can terminate the daemon instead of reporting the shutdown failure through the owning run.
findings.suggestion: Handle the abort-triggered stop rejection and propagate or record it through the owning process scope without creating an unhandled promise rejection.
findings.failure_scenario: A running preview is cancelled and descendant inspection fails during termination; serving rejects with ProcessTerminationError and the abort listener's discarded stop promise rejects unhandled.

findings.title: Preview output without newlines can exhaust daemon memory
findings.detail: The new serve path uses runConfined, which installs line callbacks through runProcess. Its lineSplitter accumulates all output until a newline without applying tailLimit. A candidate server can therefore emit an arbitrarily long line while remaining alive, causing unbounded memory growth in the factory daemon. The previous serve implementation bounded its collected output to 4,000 characters. Build and seed also pass through runSandboxed's stdout line callback and have the same exposure until they exit.
findings.suggestion: Bound the line splitter's pending buffer or use a bounded raw-chunk callback for preview output while preserving startup detection.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview serve command repeatedly writes bytes to stdout without a newline while serving requests; the daemon retains the growing line until it exhausts memory.

findings.title: Readiness deadline includes confinement verification
findings.detail: The readiness deadline starts immediately after calling runConfined, while that call is still asynchronously verifying the Seatbelt profile. Verification runs multiple subprocess probes and each can take up to 30 seconds. A slow but successful verification can therefore consume the entire 20-second readiness window before the serve command starts, causing a healthy preview to fail.
findings.suggestion: Start the readiness deadline when the confined payload starts, and retain a separate bound for confinement verification.
findings.failure_scenario: Seatbelt verification takes more than 20 seconds under load, then succeeds; the serve command has no time to bind or answer before preview readiness times out.

findings.title: Abort can leave a rejected stop promise unhandled
findings.detail: The abort listener discards the promise returned by stop(), but stop now rejects when process termination cannot be confirmed or scratch removal fails. After a preview has been returned, that rejection can occur before the engine reaches its cleanup handler, producing an unhandled rejection that can terminate the daemon instead of reporting the cleanup failure through the run.
findings.suggestion: Attach a rejection handler in the abort listener while preserving the same rejected stop promise for the owning cleanup path to await.
findings.failure_scenario: A running preview is cancelled and process inspection fails during shutdown, causing serving to reject with ProcessTerminationError while the abort listener has no rejection handler.

findings.title: Repository preview is exercised only with the fake backend
findings.detail: The repository UI preview test calls the local startPreview wrapper, which selects fakeConfinement. The real Seatbelt test uses a small fixture instead, so the tests do not establish that this repository's actual build, seed and serve commands work under the new read and write policy.
findings.suggestion: Run the repository preview test with the real Seatbelt backend on eligible macOS hosts, retaining the existing platform and nested-confinement skip.
findings.failure_scenario: The actual UI build or daemon accesses a path denied by Seatbelt: the fake-backed repository test passes, while a real preview fails.

Reviewed the merge, approval, change-view and CLI paths. The focused test command passed 62 notifier tests but could not run the MCP, CLI or land-queue tests because the MCP SDK dependency was unavailable in the environment.

findings.title: A cancelled land can be overwritten after the new metadata lookup
findings.detail: The metadata lookup adds an await after the merge succeeds. If cancellation occurs during that lookup, cancel() records the entry as cancelled and aborts the signal, but the catch converts the aborted lookup to null and landed() unconditionally changes the entry to landed. The same path can write after queue shutdown.
findings.suggestion: Re-read the entry and honor cancellation or shutdown after the lookup before finalizing it; make the state transition conditional.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub confirms the merge, the metadata request is pending, and a user cancels the land. The request aborts, then the cancelled entry becomes landed.

findings.title: A missing post-merge observation permanently leaves the feed event incomplete
findings.detail: When the post-merge lookup fails or returns an observation without metadata, this update emits run.merged with null fields. Later reconciliation updates only the run columns; the feed trigger fires only on the merged transition, so the existing event remains unchanged. With polling disabled, reconciliation also deliberately makes no fresh lookup for an already merged run, so even the run fields can stay null indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Ensure merge metadata is obtained and recorded in the merge event, and provide a bounded recovery path for missing observations that also corrects the event exposed to consumers.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds but the immediate GitHub lookup fails transiently; a later observation supplies the merger and timestamp, yet the parent run.merged feed item still reports both as null.

findings.title: The reported change-view request still cannot identify the changed head
findings.detail: The exact request in the issue, with run and file: 1 but no pagination pins, fails schema validation before the backend checks the current head. It always returns the pagination instruction, even when the saved PR head has been superseded, and does not provide the new head requested by the acceptance criteria.
findings.suggestion: Handle this request so a superseded head is identified with its current SHA before returning the pagination prerequisite, while retaining the pin requirement for actual follow-up reads.
findings.failure_scenario: After a conflict round moves the head, call limitless_get_change with {"run":"…","file":1}; the response says only that further reads require headSha and baseSha.

findings.title: A cancellation during the new metadata lookup is overwritten
findings.detail: The post-merge lookup introduces an await after the merge succeeds. If the land entry is cancelled while that lookup is in flight, cancellation aborts the signal and records the cancelled state, but the caught lookup failure still calls landed(), which unconditionally changes the entry to landed and emits a land.landed event.
findings.suggestion: After the lookup, re-read the entry and make the final transition conditional on its still being in the expected state; preserve cancellation.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds, the GitHub metadata request is pending, and a caller cancels the land entry before that request finishes.

findings.title: A failed metadata lookup permanently leaves the merge feed inaccurate
findings.detail: When the new lookup fails or returns an observation without merge metadata, landed() writes merged=true with null fields, creating the run.merged feed item immediately. Later reconciliation can update the run fields from a saved snapshot, but it does not update the already-created feed item; it also never fetches missing metadata for an already-merged run. Thus the original inaccurate feed can persist even after metadata becomes available, and run fields can remain null when no suitable saved snapshot arrives.
findings.suggestion: Ensure merge metadata can be recovered after a transient lookup failure and that the merge event presented to consumers reflects the recovered values.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds but the immediate GitHub lookup times out; a later poll observes the merger and timestamp.

With polling disabled, or without a later usable snapshot, the parent feed retains null merge fields indefinitely.

findings.title: An in-progress push can be described as the current head
findings.detail: When pushingTo is true, reviewableHead reports superseded even if the recorded SHA is still the old head. This branch then labels that recorded SHA as the current head, although the push has not established the new head. A targeted check, `bun -e 'import { reviewableHead } from "./src/integrations/mcp-head.ts"; const old = "a".repeat(40); console.log(JSON.stringify(reviewableHead(old, { sha: old, version: 1, pushing: true })))'`, returned `{"headSha":null,"problem":"superseded"}`.
findings.suggestion: Avoid naming the recorded SHA as current while a push is in progress; report that the head is changing until a new observation is available.
findings.failure_scenario: A change-view request arrives while a conflict round is pushing and the stored head still contains the previous commit. The error calls that previous commit the current head.

findings.suggestion: Persist or derive a bounded, retryable metadata reconciliation path for merged runs whose fields are missing, including when the poller is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: A merge succeeds, the subsequent GitHub metadata request times out, and no polling snapshot is available; later notifier passes skip the GitHub lookup and mergedBy and mergedAt remain null.

findings.title: Record the merge for runs outside the resolved status set
findings.detail: The queue now delegates merge recording to resolveMergedRun, which only marks succeeded, resolved, or needs_human runs as merged. Land requests do not require one of those statuses, and a run can also be cancelled while a merge is in flight. In those cases the queue finishes as landed but silently leaves the run unmerged; the previous queue path set merged on the target run regardless of status.
findings.suggestion: Preserve merge recording for every eligible target run while retaining the existing terminal status and resolution semantics.
findings.failure_scenario: A run is cancelled after its land request starts but before GitHub confirms the merge. The land entry becomes landed, while the cancelled run keeps merged=false and no run.merged event is emitted.

findings.title: A clipped credential’s final line leaks when the file has no final newline
findings.detail: The adjacent-pair check requires the pair to end in a newline. When a long credential extends beyond the hunk and its last line has no final newline, the preceding context pairs are withheld but the final removed line is not. A direct check of privatePatchLines returned hidden indexes [1, 2, 3] for a patch whose credential-bearing removed line was index 4 (`-secret-9`). The per-line and whole-patch filters do not match that fragment.
findings.suggestion: Match the final pair without requiring a trailing newline, while preserving the mapping to both patch lines, and add an end-to-end test for a clipped credential at EOF.
findings.failure_scenario: Register a ten-line credential ending in `secret-9`, store it at EOF without a final newline, then change its last line. The hunk contains only the last few credential lines, and the change view returns `-secret-9`.

findings.title: Review prompts still render multiline credentials in prefixed diffs
findings.detail: The change only applies reconstructed-side filtering to the MCP change view. Verify-change reviews also put `reviewDiff.patch` into the model prompt, where diff prefixes interrupt a multiline registered credential in the same way. The conflict-resolution first-parent patch is another diff-rendering path. Neither is protected by the new filter or listed as a follow-up, as the request requires.
findings.suggestion: Apply a shared patch-aware privacy filter to these diff outputs, or explicitly list each remaining diff-rendering path as a follow-up.
findings.failure_scenario: A verify-change review includes a file whose added lines contain a registered multiline credential. The review prompt contains both prefixed credential lines and sends them to the model.

findings.title: Review prompts still expose multiline credentials in diffs
findings.detail: The new redaction applies only to the MCP change view. Verify-change review prompts include reviewDiff.patch directly, and conflict-resolution prompts include a first-parent patch processed by literal redaction. Neither reconstructs patch sides before checking registered multiline credentials, so diff prefixes prevent a match and both credential lines can be sent to the review model. The request also covers other outputs that render diffs; no follow-up is listed for these paths.
findings.suggestion: Apply a shared multiline-aware patch redactor to both review-prompt diff paths before the patch is truncated or sent to a model, and add targeted coverage.
findings.failure_scenario: Register a credential with value `alpha-secret\nbeta-secret`, then review an external change adding those two lines. The review prompt contains `+alpha-secret` and `+beta-secret` because the intervening diff prefix defeats literal matching.

The verify-change review path passes reviewDiff.patch into the review prompt, where line-prefixed credentials do not match literal credential redaction. Targeted check: `bun -e 'import {registerCredential,redactCredentials} from "./src/util/proc.ts"; registerCredential("REVIEW_TEST", "alpha-secret
beta-secret"); const patch="@@ -0,0 +1,2 @@
+alpha-secret
+beta-secret
"; console.log(redactCredentials(patch));'` printed both `+alpha-secret` and `+beta-secret` unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Apply shared line-aware patch redaction before embedding these diffs in review prompts, or explicitly list these renderers as follow-ups as permitted by the request.

findings.title: Review prompts can still disclose multiline credentials in diffs

Conflict-resolution review diffs pass through redactGateOutput and redactPrivate, both of which match the complete credential literally; diff line prefixes interrupt that match. The resulting first-parent patch is embedded in the model prompt. The verify-change review patch is also embedded without this new filter. The request requires other diff-rendering outputs to receive the same treatment or be listed as follow-ups, and no follow-up was provided. A targeted check confirmed the redactor behavior: `bun -e 'import {registerCredential, redactCredentials} from "./src/util/proc.ts"; registerCredential("CHECK_MULTILINE", "alpha-secret\nbeta-secret"); console.log(redactCredentials("+alpha-secret\n+beta-secret"));'` printed `+alpha-secret` and `+beta-secret` on separate lines.
findings.suggestion: Apply a shared patch-aware credential filter before embedding these diffs in review prompts, or explicitly record the affected diff-rendering paths as follow-ups as permitted by the request.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential is `alpha-secret\nbeta-secret`, and a conflict-resolution first-parent diff or verify-change diff contains those lines as additions. Both halves are sent in the review prompt.

findings.title: Setup variants make routing-policy evidence ambiguous
findings.detail: Allowing `setup` creates two distinct standard single systems for the same target that both pass the production-evidence filter in `src/evals/policy.ts`. That code assumes at most one matching system per target: it passes trials from both systems to `summarize`, then takes only the first system's summary while retaining rows from both for other policy calculations. The selected evidence therefore depends on trial ordering and can mix denominators and observations from different arms, producing incorrect routing decisions.
findings.suggestion: Define which setup variant is eligible for production policy and consistently filter both systems and trial rows to that variant before selecting and summarizing evidence. Add a policy test containing both variants for one target.
findings.failure_scenario: A review eval contains standard systems for the same model with and without `setup: true`, with different pass or blocking-recall results. Policy generation accepts both, chooses the first summary, and may combine it with rows from the other system.

findings.title: Separate setup arms can be silently conflated in routing policy
findings.detail: Adding setup to system identity allows a single eval to contain both standard-prompt systems for the same target, one with setup and one without. Policy generation still assumes there is at most one eligible system per target and takes the first summary, so the generated policy silently ignores the other arm and depends on trial ordering.
findings.suggestion: Define which setup arm is eligible for routing evidence and select it explicitly, or otherwise make policy generation handle multiple eligible systems without silently choosing the first.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval compares standard reviewers for the same model with setup omitted and with setup: true. Both pass validation, but policy generation summarizes only whichever system appears first, even if the other arm has materially different results.

findings.title: Setup variants make policy select only one of two eligible systems
findings.detail: Adding setup to the system configuration allows one eval to contain standard single-review systems for the same target with and without setup. Both qualify as production routing evidence, but policy generation assumes at most one eligible system per target and takes only the first summary. The selected evidence therefore depends on system order and silently ignores the other arm.
findings.suggestion: Define which setup variant supplies routing evidence, or explicitly aggregate/select eligible systems without relying on their order.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval contains standard systems A and B for the same model, with B setting setup: true. Policy generation selects both systems but uses summarize(...)[0], so reversing A and B can change the model's routing metrics.

findings.title: Replay can label finder results as prepared when they were not
findings.detail: Setup is allowed on panel systems, including replay systems, but replay validation does not compare setup with the source system. Running setup in the new worktree cannot change the stored finder outputs that replay uses. Consequently a setup-enabled replay can report findings generated without dependencies as though its finders had reviewed the prepared worktree.
findings.suggestion: Require replay source and destination systems to have matching setup settings, or reject setup for replay systems.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel trial is recorded without setup. A later panel system sets setup: true and replays that trial; setup succeeds, but the finders' outputs still come from the unprepared source trial.

findings.title: Invocation exceptions inflate preparation time
findings.detail: Review trials do not set roundsUsed, so an exception after the reviewer starts enters this branch and overwrites preparationMs with the time since preparation began. The reported preparation time then includes the reviewer invocation and any provider wait.
findings.suggestion: Record whether preparation completed and only compute failure preparation time when the exception occurred before completion.
findings.failure_scenario: A review harness throws after running for several minutes; the error trial reports those minutes as preparation even though setup had already completed.

findings.title: Setup variants can make production policy select the wrong trial arm
findings.detail: Allowing standard-prompt systems that differ only in setup invalidates policy selection's assumption that at most one production-compatible system exists per target. `selectEvidence` counts both systems, and `generatePolicy` takes the first summary rather than choosing between them. Consequently, the generated production policy can depend on system ordering or names and use the wrong arm's scores.
findings.suggestion: Define which setup arm is valid policy evidence and filter to that arm consistently in both policy selection and generation. Add a test with both standard arms for the same target and different outcomes.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval contains standard reviewers for the same target with and without `setup: true`; their pass rates differ. Policy generation includes both and uses the first candidate summary, so renaming or ordering the systems can change the production routing decision.

findings.title: Preserve unrelated patch lines when a credential matches
findings.detail: A match anywhere in either complete file replaces the entire patch with one placeholder. This fails the acceptance criterion that the rest of the file stays visible, and can hide an unrelated change even when the credential itself is outside the displayed hunks. The new test explicitly expects the whole-file placeholder rather than checking that public lines survive.
findings.suggestion: Map matches on each reconstructed file side back to their patch lines and withhold only the affected lines before paging.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file contains public lines before and after a two-line registered credential. The returned diff contains only "[withheld: private text; 1 file]", so neither public line is available to the reviewer.

findings.title: Protect multiline credentials in review prompt patches
findings.detail: The verify-change review prompt embeds a raw line-prefixed diff, and this change neither protects that output nor lists it as a follow-up. A multiline registered credential split by diff prefixes does not match literal credential redaction, so its components can be sent to the review model. The request explicitly covers other outputs that render diffs unless identified as follow-ups.
findings.suggestion: Apply shared line-aware patch redaction before embedding the patch in a prompt, or explicitly document this output as a follow-up as permitted by the request.
findings.failure_scenario: A verify-change run reviews an added file containing a registered two-line credential; the prompt includes the two lines prefixed by '+' and literal matching does not remove them.

findings.title: Avoid refusing small diffs of large files
findings.detail: Whenever any multiline credential is registered, the new check reads each entire blob through sh, which rejects output above 50,000,000 characters. The outer catch then makes the entire change view unavailable, even if the actual diff is small and contains no private text. Previously the view only needed the bounded diff.
findings.suggestion: Inspect file content with a bounded streaming matcher, or otherwise handle oversized blobs without making unrelated small patches unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR changes one line in an existing text file larger than 50,000,000 characters while a multiline credential is registered. limitless_get_change returns "Local comparison commits or Git inspection unavailable" instead of the small patch.

findings.title: A credential match hides the entire file
findings.detail: Any multiline credential found anywhere on either file side replaces the complete patch with a single withholding marker. This fails the acceptance criterion that the rest of the file stays visible and also hides unrelated changes when the credential itself is outside the displayed hunks. The new test explicitly expects this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Map matches to the affected patch lines before paging and withhold those lines while retaining unrelated patch content.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file contains public lines before and after a registered two-line credential. The response contains only '[withheld: private text; 1 file]', so neither public line is available.

findings.title: Diff-formatted report text can still disclose multiline credentials
findings.detail: The new file-side check applies only to the diff field. Persisted reports are still passed through literal privacy matching, which cannot recognize a registered multiline credential when each line has a diff prefix. A report containing such a patch is returned through the reports pages with both credential lines intact. The request also covers other outputs that render diffs.
findings.suggestion: Apply prefix-aware multiline credential filtering to diff-formatted report content, or explicitly document this output as a follow-up as requested.
findings.failure_scenario: A persisted report includes '+alpha-secret\n+beta-secret' and 'alpha-secret\nbeta-secret' is registered as a credential. Reading the report page returns both prefixed lines.

findings.title: A credential match withholds the entire file
findings.detail: A match on either file side replaces the complete patch with a single placeholder. This fails the request's explicit requirement to hide only the lines spanned by the credential and leave the rest of the file visible. The added tests assert this whole-file behavior.
findings.suggestion: Map matches on each reconstructed file side back to affected patch lines and withhold those lines before paging, preserving unrelated lines.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file contains a two-line registered credential followed by ordinary implementation code. The response contains only `[withheld: private text; 1 file]`, so none of the ordinary code can be reviewed.

findings.title: Line-prefixed credentials remain visible in persisted reports
findings.detail: The new matching only protects the selected file patch. Persisted reports still pass through literal privacy matching, which does not reconstruct quoted or diff-prefixed lines. The request explicitly includes other line-prefixed outputs or requires them to be listed as follow-ups; neither happens here.
findings.suggestion: Apply line-aware credential filtering to report content before paging, including quoted and diff-prefixed text, or explicitly document the remaining outputs as follow-ups as requested.
findings.failure_scenario: A persisted implementer summary contains a diff with `+alpha-secret` and `+beta-secret` on consecutive lines, and the registered credential is `alpha-secret\nbeta-secret`. Literal matching misses the inserted prefixes and `reports[].text` returns both halves.

findings.title: Large files make small diffs unavailable when a multiline credential is registered
findings.detail: The new check reads each complete blob through `worktreeGit`, whose output is limited to 50,000,000 characters. A small patch to a larger text file previously required only the bounded diff output; now the full-blob read throws and the catch returns an unavailable response.
findings.suggestion: Inspect large blobs with bounded streaming or another approach that can scan the full content without requiring it to fit in subprocess output memory.
findings.failure_scenario: With any multiline credential registered, a one-line change to a text file larger than 50 million characters causes `limitless_get_change` to return `Local comparison commits or Git inspection unavailable`.

findings.title: A passing retry can clear a security check failure
findings.detail: The retry classification treats every configured check alike: a successful full retry becomes a nonblocking flaky result. GateCommand has no security classification, and this path has no guard preserving a security check's failure. That leaves the request's explicit security-check requirement unmet.
findings.suggestion: Provide a trusted way to identify security checks and keep their original failure blocking even when a retry passes; cover both baseline and post-change behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured security check passes on baseline, fails after a change, and passes on its full retry. It is classified flaky and nonblocking despite the original security failure.

findings.title: Incomplete nested failure reports can be accepted as complete
findings.detail: A suite reporting failures without a file is accepted whenever it has any nested suite, even if its reported failure is not represented by a nested failing testcase. If another nested suite supplies a valid failing file, the parser returns that partial list. A failing targeted retry then stops the full retry, so the unaccounted failure is never confirmed.
findings.suggestion: Verify that reported suite failure and error counts are accounted for by identifiable failures, and fall back to the full retry when they are not.
findings.failure_scenario: A parent suite reports two failures, one nested suite identifies a failing file, and another suite-level error has no file. Parsing returns only the known file; if that file fails on retry, the full check is skipped despite the incomplete failure list.

findings.title: Changed-file failures bypass the targeted retry
findings.detail: The existing pointsAt guard excludes a regression before the new targeted retry logic can inspect its structured failure files. A test failure that names a changed file is therefore never confirmed, even when its failing test file is known. This misses the requested targeted retry for a common regression scenario and can leave a transient failure classified as a blocking regression. A focused reproduction using retryRegressions returned {"calls":0,"verdict":"regressed"} when the failure output named the changed test file.
findings.suggestion: Allow failures with valid structured test files through to the targeted retry; retain the existing changed-file behavior for failures whose files cannot be determined if that behavior is still required.

output.summary:
Reviewed the listener, pairing, credential protection, heartbeat, and startup paths. The request permits splitting off gate jobs, so this review treats pairing and heartbeats as the first slice. The targeted command `bun test test/workers.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing `@simplewebauthn/server`.

Reviewed the listener, pairing, heartbeat, credential protection and restart paths. The pairing and credential isolation issues need changes. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout's available dependencies lack @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js and provide a Zod version without number().overwrite().

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker prints a code supplied by that connection before pinning its certificate. A network attacker can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, forward its code and pairing secret to the worker, and proxy the claim. The owner sees matching codes and approves, while the attacker learns the issued worker token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.
findings.suggestion: Bind the code verified by the owner to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, so a relay using a different certificate produces a different code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, relays the genuine request and code, and obtains the approved token despite the owner comparing the displayed codes.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not protected in other factory processes
findings.detail: Private-file protection is held in a process-local map and is released when pairing exits. Running the worker registers the paths only in the worker CLI process, not in a separate daemon on the same machine. That daemon's agent sandboxes therefore do not add the worker token or coordinator fingerprint to their deny lists. The same problem applies to an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every factory process that builds agent sandbox policies, independently of whether the worker or listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is paired as a worker and also runs a factory daemon; an agent launched by that daemon can read the worker token because the pairing process's private-path registration is not shared.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation prevents subsequent daemon starts
findings.detail: Certificate creation first publishes an empty key file and then runs OpenSSL. If the process stops or OpenSSL fails before both files are created, the next startup treats the remaining file as incomplete material and throws. Because the worker listener starts as part of daemon startup, this prevents the whole daemon from starting until the files are repaired manually.
findings.suggestion: Generate the key and certificate in temporary files and publish the completed pair safely, with recovery for interrupted first-time creation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL creates cert.pem; every subsequent start with the worker listener enabled fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The first TLS connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. An active intermediary can forward the pairing request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and learn the pairing secret. The owner sees the same code and approves, after which the intermediary can claim the worker token. Pinning the intermediary's certificate on later requests does not detect this relay.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verifiable pairing code to the actual coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS endpoint changes the code or otherwise fails verification.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's initial connection, proxies pairing to the coordinator, and observes the returned secret while relaying the matching code to both parties.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to agents in other processes
findings.detail: Private-file protection is an in-memory registry. The pairing command releases its registrations on return, and the worker process registers its files only in its own process. A separate factory daemon on the same machine therefore does not add the worker token or pinned fingerprint to its agent read-deny policy. findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently prevents startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key file before invoking OpenSSL. If the process is interrupted or OpenSSL fails before both files are complete, the next start encounters an incomplete pair and throws instead of recovering. An empty or partially written pair can likewise fail when parsed. Because the listener starts during daemon startup, this can prevent the daemon from starting until someone manually repairs the files.
findings.suggestion: Generate the pair in temporary files and publish it only after validating both files, with recovery for an interrupted first generation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after key.pem is created but before cert.pem is written; every subsequent start with the worker listener configured fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

findings.title: Pairing expiry depends on synchronized machine clocks
findings.detail: The coordinator returns an absolute expiry in its own clock, but the worker compares it directly to its local clock. A worker whose clock is ahead can stop polling immediately even though the coordinator has accepted a valid pending request; the owner can approve it but the worker never claims the token.
findings.suggestion: Use a relative lifetime or let the coordinator enforce expiry while the worker polls with a locally measured deadline.
findings.failure_scenario: The worker clock is more than ten minutes ahead of the coordinator when pairing begins; the worker prints the code and immediately reports `Pairing expired`.

findings.title: Default worker name can be rejected by the pairing schema
findings.detail: The default name is the operating system hostname, but the server accepts only ASCII letters, digits, underscores, periods and hyphens. A valid local hostname containing another character causes the documented pairing command to fail unless the user discovers and supplies a compatible `--name`.
findings.suggestion: Normalize the default name to the accepted format or validate it locally and explain how to select a valid name.
findings.failure_scenario: A Mac reports a hostname containing a space or non-ASCII character; `limitless worker pair --coordinator ...` receives HTTP 400.

findings.title: An approved worker can become permanently unable to claim its token
findings.detail: The claim deadline still applies after approval, but an approved row is never expired or replaced by a new pairing request. If approval occurs near the deadline and the worker is disconnected until after it, the claim is rejected and a new pairing using the same name is also rejected. Recovery requires the owner to discover and revoke the stranded approved entry.
findings.suggestion: Provide a recoverable transition for an approved pairing whose token was never claimed, or allow a fresh pairing without leaving the name permanently blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request at 9 minutes 59 seconds; the worker's next claim arrives after 10 minutes and receives an error. Re-running pairing with the same name fails because the row remains approved.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation leaves TLS startup unrecoverable
findings.detail: The key file is created before OpenSSL runs, but failed or interrupted generation does not remove the partial files. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient generation failure requires manual cleanup before the listener or worker pairing can start.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful validation, cleaning up partial output on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: OpenSSL is interrupted after the empty key file is created and before the certificate is written. Every subsequent listener start fails with incomplete TLS material.

findings.title: Verify the worker checkout SHA after gates run
findings.detail: The worker records HEAD before running any setup or check commands and submits that earlier SHA with the result. Gate commands can alter the checkout, including replacing its .git file with a repository inside the writable checkout. The coordinator therefore accepts results as evidence for the requested head even when later checks ran against a different HEAD. The local pipeline explicitly checks HEAD after gates for this reason.
findings.suggestion: Re-read and verify HEAD after all gate commands finish, before posting the result; treat a changed or unverifiable HEAD as an infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command replaces .git with a new repository and changes HEAD; subsequent checks pass there, but the worker posts the original pre-setup SHA and the coordinator accepts the run for the requested commit.

findings.title: Resume discards LAN jobs for timeout and retry executions
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial and rebase handles are reattached. If the daemon restarts while a timeout rerun or baseline/regression retry is leased, the persisted handle is instead cancelled and a new job is enqueued. This breaks the durable start/attach contract and can repeat a gate that already completed on a worker.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry state to resume every LAN execution from its existing handle, including timeout and targeted retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon shuts down after starting a `regression-retry` job but before receiving its result. On resume, the purpose is excluded from the allowlist, so the old job is cancelled and the retry starts again.

findings.title: A final result can contradict a previously reported failed check
findings.detail: Check events are validated and stored independently of the final GateRun. The final result is accepted solely by matching its own check names and commands; it is never reconciled with the events already received for that lease. A worker can report a failing check and then submit a passing result for the same check, causing the coordinator to grade the job as passing.
findings.suggestion: Track check events per lease attempt and reject a final result that contradicts the completed checks, treating the contradiction as an infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid event for requested check `test` with `ok: false`, then posts a valid final GateRun containing the same check with `ok: true` and exit code zero. The final result is accepted and the failing check becomes a pass.

findings.title: Infrastructure retry can discard an already observed failing check
findings.detail: Check events from an abandoned worker attempt are retained only as events. If that attempt later loses its lease or fails to report its final result, the executor returns the later worker or local result without incorporating the previously observed failure. A passing rerun can therefore make a failing check appear clean.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and reconcile completed check results across infrastructure attempts so a previously observed failure cannot become a clean pass.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing check event, disconnects before posting its GateRun, and the local fallback passes the same check. The executor returns the passing fallback result.

findings.title: Accepting reordered checks can associate retry results with the wrong checks
findings.detail: The validator checks membership and uniqueness but does not require the requested order. The retry code in run.ts associates returned checks with original failures by array index, so an untrusted worker can return the correct checks in reverse order and cause one check's result to be applied to another.
findings.suggestion: Validate each returned check against the corresponding requested check in order, or change all consumers to associate retry results by validated identity.
findings.failure_scenario: Two failed checks are retried together; a worker returns the second check's passing result first and the first check's failing result second. The first regression is classified as flaky using the other check's pass.

findings.title: A retry can erase a check failure reported before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from an abandoned lease are retained, but the executor returns only the final attempt's GateRun. A failed check reported by the first worker is therefore discarded for grading if that worker subsequently loses its lease and the next attempt passes. The gate is graded as a clean pass even though a requested check failed, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Carry completed check outcomes across infrastructure attempts and preserve a prior failure in the final grading, including when falling back locally.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts a failing check event and disconnects before posting its final result; worker B runs the same job and posts a passing result. The pipeline receives only worker B's passing GateRun.

findings.title: Restart discards durable LAN jobs for retry and timeout executions
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are reattached. A coordinator restart while a timeout rerun or a targeted/full check retry is leased causes the persisted handle to be cancelled and a new job to be enqueued when the stage resumes. This violates the requested restart behavior and can repeat gate side effects despite the original job still running.
findings.suggestion: Provide a durable resume path for every LAN execution purpose, preserving the inputs and prior stage evidence needed to reattach safely.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a worker is executing a `timeout` gate job. On resume the pending handle fails the purpose check, is cancelled, and another job is started.

findings.title: Allow the Bun executable the verifier will actually invoke
findings.detail: The read exception is based on the daemon’s `process.execPath`, but a verifier running `bun test` resolves `bun` from its shell PATH. Those can be different installations, including when the daemon is started with an absolute Bun path or the shell selects a project-local Bun. If the selected executable is under a denied private root, it remains unreadable and the verifier still cannot run tests. The new smoke check also invokes `process.execPath` explicitly, so it can pass while the verifier’s ordinary `bun test` fails.
findings.suggestion: Resolve and validate the Bun executable using the environment the verifier’s shell will use, and have the live probe exercise `bun test` through that same PATH.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts with `/opt/homebrew/bin/bun`, while the verifier’s PATH selects `~/.bun/bin/bun`. The sandbox allows the former and denies reads under the home directory, so the verifier’s `bun test` cannot execute even though the smoke probe uses the allowed executable.

findings.title: Smoke probe does not exercise the production verifier configuration
findings.detail: The probe sets confineReads to true and invokes process.execPath directly. The production verify stage does not set confineReads, so it receives the configured slotted command wrappers instead. Consequently, the smoke check bypasses the wrapper and lease-connection behavior involved in ordinary verifier commands, and the Bun read allowance it exercises is not applied to that verifier path. It can pass while an actual verifier's bun test still hangs.
findings.suggestion: Run the live probe through the same configuration and slotted-command setup used by the verify stage, invoking bun test through the verifier's PATH. Keep a separate confined-reader probe if that path also needs coverage.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier runs bun test through a slotted wrapper that stalls acquiring a lease, while the smoke probe runs the absolute Bun executable without that wrapper and reports success.

Reviewed the publication rewrite and its delivery and land call sites. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency. A standalone reproduction of the rewrite confirmed the path-matching defects below.

Reviewed the publication rewrite and its delivery and landing callers. The focused Bun test could not start because the checkout has no node_modules and cannot resolve entities; a direct execution of the rewrite function reproduced a privacy leak.

findings.title: Absolute paths in link labels bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The Markdown-link alternative consumes the entire link, but examines only its destination. If the destination is an ordinary relative or web link, the original link is returned unchanged, including any local path in its visible label. This can publish the owner's username and data layout or cause delivery to fail once the username is added to private strings.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path occurrences in link labels independently of the destination while preserving ordinary link destinations.
findings.failure_scenario: `[/factory/data/work/run/src/a.ts](src/a.ts)` is published unchanged when `/factory/data/work/run` is the worktree.

findings.title: Bare paths immediately following a colon are missed
findings.detail: The negative lookbehind excludes a colon, so a common `path:/absolute/path` form is not rewritten. A standalone reproduction of the expression returned `path:/factory/data/work/run/file.ts` unchanged. The original absolute path can therefore reach a public report or block delivery under the private-strings check.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local roots after a colon while separately protecting actual URL destinations from rewriting.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer report contains `path:/factory/data/work/run/file.ts` with `/factory/data/work/run` as its worktree.

findings.title: Normalize traversal before deciding whether a path is inside the worktree
findings.detail: The prefix check treats lexical descendants as worktree files even when `..` resolves outside the worktree. It consequently emits a repo-relative link to a path outside the repository instead of the required plain `<data>` placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize absolute path components before checking directory containment and constructing the replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `[log](/factory/data/work/run/../other/log.txt)` becomes `[../other/log.txt](../other/log.txt)` rather than `<data>/work/other/log.txt`.

findings.title: Absolute paths in link labels and titles bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback checks only its destination. If that destination is already relative or is a web URL, the original link is returned unchanged, including any absolute path in its label or title. This can publish the owner's username or cause delivery to be blocked once that username is added to private strings. A direct check using `bun -e 'const s = await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); const f = s.slice(s.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"), s.indexOf("/** Check both")); const js = new Bun.Transpiler({loader:"ts"}).transformSync(f.replace("export function", "function") + "\nreturn sanitizePublication;"); const sanitize = new Function(js)(); const w="/factory/data/work/run", d="/factory/data"; for (const t of [`[${w}/file.ts](file.ts)`, `[link](https://example.com "${w}/file.ts")`]) console.log(JSON.stringify([t,sanitize(t,w,d)]));'` returned `["[/factory/data/work/run/file.ts](file.ts)","[/factory/data/work/run/file.ts](file.ts)"]` and `["[link](https://example.com \"/factory/data/work/run/file.ts\")","[link](https://example.com \"/factory/data/work/run/file.ts\")"]`.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize local paths in link labels and titles as well as destinations, while preserving ordinary links.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer writes `[/Users/name/.limitless/work/run/file.ts](file.ts)` in a report; the absolute path remains in the published body or comment.

findings.title: Round delivery rewrites the existing PR body
findings.detail: The code applies publicationText to the concatenation of the existing PR body and the new round section. Consequently, adding a round can replace paths already present in the published body, including paths in text written by a person. Rewriting already published PR bodies is explicitly outside the request.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize the new section before appending it, without transforming the existing body.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing PR body contains a link to an earlier run under the factory data directory; delivery of a review round replaces that link with a `<data>` placeholder.
