findings.title: Absolute paths in link labels and titles bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback checks only its destination. If that destination is already relative or is a web URL, the original link is returned unchanged, including any absolute path in its label or title. This can publish the owner's username or cause delivery to be blocked once that username is added to private strings. A direct check using `bun -e 'const s = await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); const f = s.slice(s.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"), s.indexOf("/** Check both")); const js = new Bun.Transpiler({loader:"ts"}).transformSync(f.replace("export function", "function") + "\nreturn sanitizePublication;"); const sanitize = new Function(js)(); const w="/factory/data/work/run", d="/factory/data"; for (const t of [`[${w}/file.ts](file.ts)`, `[link](https://example.com "${w}/file.ts")`]) console.log(JSON.stringify([t,sanitize(t,w,d)]));'` returned `["[/factory/data/work/run/file.ts](file.ts)","[/factory/data/work/run/file.ts](file.ts)"]` and `["[link](https://example.com \"/factory/data/work/run/file.ts\")","[link](https://example.com \"/factory/data/work/run/file.ts\")"]`.

The shared sanitizer misses some local paths and rewrites previously published PR content. Focused tests could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency; a standalone invocation of the sanitizer reproduced the path leaks.

findings.title: Absolute paths in link labels bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The regex consumes a whole Markdown link, but the replacement checks only its destination. If the destination is relative, an absolute worktree or data-directory path in the label is published unchanged. Once the username is added to private-strings.txt, the privacy check will instead block delivery. A direct sanitizer check returned `[/factory/data/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing link text as well as destinations, including when the destination itself requires no rewrite.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[/factory/data/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` and the configured worktree is `/factory/data/work/run`.

findings.title: File-URL links retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: The destination comparison requires the path to start with a configured root, so a `file://` URL pointing into the worktree is left unchanged. The entire Markdown link is consumed before the bare-path matcher can inspect it. A direct sanitizer check returned `[x](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` unchanged, exposing the local path or blocking delivery when the username is private.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URLs and normalize their path before applying the worktree and data-directory rules.
findings.failure_scenario: A model reports `[x](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` for a file in the run's worktree.

findings.title: Parent-directory paths are classified as worktree files
findings.detail: The prefix comparison does not resolve `..` segments before deciding which root contains a path. The direct check rewrote `[x](/factory/data/work/run/../secret)` to `[../secret](../secret)`, although the target is outside the worktree and should be plain text under `<data>`.
findings.suggestion: Normalize path segments before selecting the containing root, while preserving any Markdown suffix that is not part of the filesystem path.
findings.failure_scenario: A report links `/factory/data/work/run/../secret`, where the worktree is `/factory/data/work/run` and the data directory is `/factory/data`.

findings.title: Markdown links can retain absolute paths in their labels and file URLs
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes a whole Markdown link, but the callback examines only its destination. An absolute path in the label is therefore never sanitized when the destination is relative. A file:// destination also fails the root-prefix comparison. Either form can publish the owner's absolute path or cause the private-strings check to block delivery. The following targeted command reproduced both results: `bun -e 'const t=await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); const s=new Function(new Bun.Transpiler({loader:"ts"}).transformSync(t.slice(t.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"),t.indexOf("/** Check both"))).replace("export ","")+";return sanitizePublication")(); console.log(s("[/data/work/r/a.ts](a.ts) [a](file:///data/work/r/a.ts)","/data/work/r","/data"));'` Output: `[/data/work/r/a.ts](a.ts) [a](file:///data/work/r/a.ts)`.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing link labels as well as destinations, and recognize local file URLs before comparing their paths with the configured roots.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[/data/work/r/a.ts](a.ts)` or `[a](file:///data/work/r/a.ts)` and is published with the absolute local path intact.

findings.title: Round delivery rewrites the existing published PR body
findings.detail: The sanitizer is applied to `pr.body + text`, so appending a review round also changes any matching paths in the previously published body. The request explicitly excludes rewriting already published PR bodies, and this can alter text written or edited by a PR participant.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize the new round section before appending it, while preserving the existing PR body.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing PR body contains a local path, and a review round is appended; the edit silently rewrites that existing content.

findings.title: Paths containing parent traversal are classified by their spelling
findings.detail: The prefix comparison treats a path beginning with the worktree root as inside the worktree even when `..` resolves outside it. For example, `/factory/data/work/run/../other/log.txt` becomes `../other/log.txt` instead of a `<data>` path.
findings.suggestion: Normalize local paths before determining which root contains them, while preserving any Markdown fragment or line suffix separately.
findings.failure_scenario: A report references a sibling run using a path through the current worktree and the published result is a broken relative path rather than the required data-directory placeholder.

findings.title: Image references become ordinary links
findings.detail: The link matcher accepts the leading `!` of an image, but the replacement always emits ordinary link syntax. A report image pointing into the worktree consequently stops rendering in the published report.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the image marker when rewriting a worktree image destination.
findings.failure_scenario: `![alt](/factory/data/work/run/img.png)` is published as `[img.png](img.png)`.

output.summary:
The new checks protect several outcome writes, but claim loss can still be followed by a merge, a push, or removal of the new worker’s checkout. The targeted command `bun test test/land-queue.test.ts` could not run: Bun reported one error because a dependency was missing.

Reviewed the claim checks, CI inspection, and worktree lifecycle. The targeted command `bun test test/land-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; it reported 0 passing tests and one module-resolution error.

findings.title: Recheck ownership inside the merge operation before issuing the command
findings.detail: The ownership check precedes the call to mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing `gh pr merge` and can perform further awaits during retries. A reclaim during one of those awaits does not abort the old worker until its next heartbeat, so it can still issue a merge after losing its claim. The check after mergePullRequest returns is too late to prevent it.
findings.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the merge helper and check it immediately before each merge attempt, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest and waits for `gh pr view`; another owner reclaims the entry; the view returns before the heartbeat and the old worker issues `gh pr merge`.

findings.title: Guard the actual push after the helper's asynchronous preparation
findings.detail: pushExistingBranch awaits rev-parse, transport setup, ls-remote and an ancestry check before issuing the push. The claim can be reclaimed during any of those awaits, after the queue's ownership transaction has completed. The old worker can then push before its heartbeat detects the loss.
findings.suggestion: Check ownership immediately before the actual push within the helper, after its asynchronous preparation.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker passes the ownership check, pauses in pushExistingBranch's ls-remote, and is reclaimed. When ls-remote returns before the next heartbeat, the old worker pushes its merge commit.

findings.title: Do not discard a reclaimed worker's shared checkout
findings.detail: Every attempt uses the same `land-<entry id>` worktree path, and the old worker unconditionally discards it in finally even when an ownership check detects a reclaim. If the new owner has already recreated that checkout, the old worker removes the new owner's worktree and files, disrupting its checks or merge.
findings.suggestion: Give attempts distinct checkout paths or otherwise make cleanup conditional on ownership of the specific checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A second worker reclaims an entry and creates its checkout while the first worker is awaiting CI. The first worker's CI response returns, its claim check fails, and its finally block removes the second worker's checkout.

findings.title: CI inspection can persist results after the claim is reclaimed
findings.detail: Passing `current` to `ciDecision` does not guard all of its writes. For example, after awaiting the default-branch checks, the classifier emits CI feed items and updates `ci.main` before it calls `current()`. It also writes a rerun outcome after awaiting the rerun request without rechecking ownership. The later check in the queue cannot undo those writes.
findings.suggestion: Make the classifier's land-triggered writes conditional on claim ownership in the same transaction, including writes following CI reads and rerun responses.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker awaits a default-branch CI response or a rerun response; another owner reclaims the entry before that response arrives. The old worker then updates CI state or emits a feed item despite having lost the claim.

findings.title: Recheck the claim inside the merge helper before issuing the command
findings.detail: The ownership check happens before calling mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing `gh pr merge`, and it can repeat that sequence during retries. The heartbeat may not have fired when the lookup returns, so a worker that lost its claim can still issue the merge.
findings.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the helper and check it immediately before every merge attempt, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest and waits for `gh pr view`; another owner reclaims the entry; the view returns before the next heartbeat, and the old worker issues `gh pr merge`.

findings.title: Recheck ownership immediately before the actual push
findings.detail: pushExistingBranch performs several awaited operations after the queue's ownership check, including remote and ancestry lookups, before spawning the push. A reclaim during one of those awaits leaves the signal live until the heartbeat, so the old worker can push after losing its claim.
findings.suggestion: Provide a claim guard to the push path and invoke it immediately before spawning the push.
findings.failure_scenario: The entry is reclaimed while the old worker awaits `git ls-remote` inside pushExistingBranch; that command returns before the next heartbeat, and the old worker pushes the merge commit.

findings.title: Guard CI inspection writes after its awaited requests
findings.detail: Passing `current` to ciDecision does not guard every write. For example, inspectCi awaits the default branch checks and then emits CI events and updates `ci.main:<repo>` before checking `current`; requestRerun also writes its outcome after awaiting the request without rechecking. These writes can therefore occur after a reclaim.
findings.suggestion: Make the CI inspection's claim-sensitive writes conditional on ownership in the same transaction, including rerun outcomes.
findings.failure_scenario: A failing CI inspection waits for default-branch check results, the entry is reclaimed, and the response arrives before heartbeat; the old inspection writes a CI event and repository setting despite no longer owning the claim.

findings.title: Do not let a displaced worker remove the new worker's checkout
findings.detail: The finally block always discards the deterministic `land-<entry id>` worktree. Both claimants use that same path, so after a reclaim the old worker can remove the checkout that the new worker has already created. The new worker may then fail and block the land or lose its in-progress work.
findings.suggestion: Give each claim an isolated checkout and clean up only that claim's checkout, or otherwise coordinate cleanup so a displaced worker cannot remove its successor's files.
findings.failure_scenario: A new owner reclaims the entry and recreates its worktree while the old worker is awaiting a CI or merge response; the old worker detects claim loss and its finally block deletes the new owner's worktree.

findings.title: CI inspection can write after the claim is reclaimed
findings.detail: The ownership callback passed to `ciDecision` is not checked before every write. `inspectCi` awaits the default-branch check runs, then emits CI feed items and updates the `ci.main` setting before calling `current()`. Its rerun response handler also writes outcomes after an await without rechecking ownership. A reclaimed worker can therefore still change durable CI state.
findings.suggestion: Make the claim check atomic with each CI inspection write, including writes following a rerun response, or stop the inspection before those writes when the claim is lost.
findings.failure_scenario: A failing CI inspection is waiting for the default-branch check-runs response when another worker reclaims the entry. Releasing the response lets the old worker update `ci.main` and potentially emit `ci.main_red` before it notices the lost claim.

findings.title: A worker that loses its claim can delete the new worker’s checkout
findings.detail: The unconditional `finally` cleanup uses a worktree path based only on the entry ID. After a reclaim, the new worker uses that same path, so the old worker can remove the new worker’s worktree when its pending operation completes and claim validation throws.
findings.suggestion: Give each claim its own worktree path, or coordinate cleanup so a worker cannot remove a checkout belonging to a newer claim.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker is waiting for CI; a new owner reclaims the entry and creates `land-<id>`. The old CI response arrives, `assertClaim` throws, and the old worker’s `finally` removes the new owner’s checkout while it is running checks.

findings.title: A worker that lost its claim can still write the shared gate log
findings.detail: Gate results append to a path shared by every attempt without checking claim ownership. The initial log write is also unguarded. If another worker reclaims the entry while a gate is running, the old worker can append its results after the replacement has started and written its own log. The replacement’s recorded log can then contain results from both attempts, contrary to the requirement that a worker which lost its claim writes nothing.
findings.suggestion: Give each attempt a separate log path and guard writes made after asynchronous work against loss of the claim.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A is awaiting a gate result when worker B reclaims the entry and starts checks. B truncates and writes `land-<id>.log`; before A’s next heartbeat, A’s gate result invokes `onResult` and appends stale output to B’s log.

findings.title: Recheck ownership on every push retry
findings.detail: The claim guard runs once before `remoteSh`, but `remoteSh` retries transient failures internally after an awaited delay. A claim can be reclaimed during the first push or retry delay, and the old worker will issue another push without checking ownership.
findings.suggestion: Run the guard immediately before each push attempt inside the retry callback.
findings.failure_scenario: The first push fails transiently, another worker reclaims the entry during the retry delay, and the old worker starts a second push before its heartbeat aborts it.

findings.title: Prevent stale workers from writing the shared gate log
findings.detail: Gate result callbacks append to a log path shared by every attempt without checking claim ownership. A replacement attempt also truncates that same file. An old gate result arriving after reclaim can therefore append stale output to the replacement's log, contrary to the requirement that a worker that lost its claim writes nothing.
findings.suggestion: Guard gate log writes with claim ownership and isolate the log path by attempt so overlapping workers cannot corrupt each other's evidence.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate remains in flight while the entry is reclaimed and the replacement starts checks; the old gate then reports a result and appends its output to the replacement attempt's log.

findings.title: A rejected rerun can remain pending forever after claim loss
findings.detail: The rerun is durably marked `rerun_requested` before the HTTP request. If the land claim is lost while that request is in flight, the new guard discards even a definitive rejection response. Subsequent inspections treat the marker as pending and only resolve it when a later workflow attempt appears. A rejected request creates no later attempt, so the replacement worker waits until its CI deadline and blocks the land instead of recording the rejection and reporting the failure.
findings.suggestion: Provide a recovery path for an unconfirmed rerun request that can distinguish a rejected request from an accepted rerun without allowing the stale worker to write after losing its claim.
findings.failure_scenario: A transient CI failure triggers a rerun request; another owner reclaims the land entry before GitHub responds with HTTP 403. The old worker discards the response, and the new worker repeatedly sees `rerun_requested` with the original workflow attempt unchanged.

findings.title: A reclaimed worker can still write into the replacement worker’s gate log
findings.detail: Gate result callbacks append to a log shared by all attempts without checking claim ownership. A worker whose claim was reclaimed while a gate was running can append its results after the replacement worker has started and written to the same file. The replacement entry can then point at a log containing output from both attempts, violating the requirement that a worker that lost its claim writes nothing and making the recorded gate evidence misleading.
findings.suggestion: Guard gate-log writes against claim loss and isolate log files by attempt so an older worker cannot modify the replacement attempt’s log.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A starts a gate, its claim expires, and worker B reclaims the entry and begins checks. Before A’s next heartbeat, A’s gate completes and its onResult callback appends to the same `land-<id>.log` used by B.

findings.title: Merged-entry recovery leaves the previous attempt’s worktree behind
findings.detail: Worktrees are now named by attempt, but the recovery path for an already merged PR discards only the newly claimed attempt’s path. It returns before checkout’s cleanup of older attempt paths, so the worktree left by the interrupted attempt and its Git registration remain indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Clean up older attempt worktrees on the merged recovery path as well, while preserving the isolation between concurrent attempts.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker merges the PR and crashes before its cleanup. The next worker claims the entry with an incremented attempt number, observes the PR as merged, and discards the nonexistent new-attempt path instead of the old worktree.

findings.title: Accept the documented PR-number target for unowned lands
findings.detail: The new path accepts only a full GitHub URL, although the land command accepts a PR number for factory-owned PRs and the request calls for `limitless land <pr> --sha <full sha>`. An unowned PR supplied as `123` or `#123` is rejected as `run not found`.
findings.suggestion: Resolve supported PR-number targets against a configured repository, with a clear ambiguity error when necessary.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator runs `limitless land 123 --sha <current-full-sha>` for an open hand-made PR on a configured repository.

findings.title: Support open PRs from forks
findings.detail: The new path rejects every cross-repository PR. The request covers open PRs on configured GitHub repositories and does not exclude fork contributions, so a common class of hand-made PR cannot use the confined land queue.
findings.suggestion: Handle fork head repositories safely through the same pinned-head and confined-check workflow.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens an otherwise valid PR from a fork into a configured repository and an operator requests a land at its current full SHA.

findings.title: Preserve pending unowned lands across rollback
findings.detail: The empty-string sentinel keeps the old schema writable, but the previous daemon interprets it as a run ID. After rollback, it claims an active unowned entry, fails to find that run, and marks the entry blocked. The pending land therefore cannot resume when the new release returns.
findings.suggestion: Use a backward-compatible representation or quarantine mechanism that prevents an older daemon from consuming unowned entries while preserving their progress.
findings.failure_scenario: A new daemon queues or starts an unowned land, then deployment rolls back to the previous release before it completes.

findings.title: Revalidate the PR base before merging
findings.detail: The base branch is captured at request time and later used to choose both the base merge and the confined checks, but the merge path does not verify that GitHub still targets that branch. Changing a PR's base does not change its head SHA, so the head pin does not catch this. GitHub can squash-merge into the new base after checks from the old base ran.
findings.suggestion: Verify the current PR base against the checked base at the merge boundary and block or restart checks if it changed.
findings.failure_scenario: A queued hand-made PR is retargeted from `main` to `release` while its head remains unchanged; the queue checks `main` and merges the PR into `release`.

findings.title: PR numbers are rejected for unowned pull requests
findings.detail: The new path accepts only a full GitHub URL, although the land command accepts PR numbers and the request calls for `limitless land <pr> --sha <full sha>`. The added test explicitly expects a bare number to fail.
findings.suggestion: Resolve a PR number to a configured repository when it can be identified unambiguously, and report ambiguity clearly when it cannot.
findings.failure_scenario: With one configured GitHub repository, `limitless land 77 --sha <current-head>` returns `run not found` for an open PR that has no factory run.

findings.title: Open fork pull requests are excluded
findings.detail: The request covers open PRs on configured repositories without restricting their head repository, but this check rejects every cross-repository PR. Fork PRs are a normal way for people to contribute to a configured repository.

findings.title: Fork pull requests are rejected
findings.detail: The new path rejects every cross-repository PR, although the request covers open PRs on configured repositories without excluding fork PRs. A fork PR targets the configured repository but cannot enter the land queue.

findings.title: Rollback blocks active unowned entries
findings.detail: Unowned entries are stored with an empty run ID. On rollback, the previous release reads that value as a run ID and its land context lookup fails because no such run exists. Consequently, an entry interrupted by a deploy or rollback is marked blocked instead of resuming, contrary to the required compatibility with the previous release.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible representation and processing strategy for active unowned entries.
findings.failure_scenario: An unowned land is waiting for CI when a deployment rolls back to the previous release; the old queue claims the entry and blocks it with "run  is gone".

findings.title: Unowned PR numbers are not accepted
findings.detail: The CLI advertises and the request specifies a PR target, but the unowned path accepts only a full GitHub URL. Bare PR numbers and #number forms resolve only through factory runs, so the same invocation that works for a factory PR fails for an unowned PR.
findings.suggestion: Resolve PR numbers against an unambiguous configured repository, or otherwise provide the repository context needed to resolve them.
findings.failure_scenario: Running `limitless land 604 --sha <full-sha>` for an unowned PR returns "run not found" even when its repository is configured.

findings.title: Unowned PRs cannot be requested by the documented PR number form
findings.detail: The existing CLI accepts a PR number, but the new unowned path accepts only a full GitHub URL. A number with no matching factory run is rejected as “run not found,” even when the PR exists on a configured repository.
findings.suggestion: Resolve supported PR references to an unambiguous configured repository and canonical URL before entering the unowned flow, or provide an explicit repository-qualified form.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless land 77 --sha <full-sha>` for an open unowned PR; the request is rejected before GitHub is queried.

findings.title: Rollback blocks active unowned lands
findings.detail: Unowned entries are persisted with an empty run ID. After a rollback, the previous release reads that value as a normal run ID; its land queue looks up the empty ID, throws “run  is gone,” and marks the entry blocked. An interrupted or queued land therefore cannot survive a rollback to the previous release.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-skew strategy that prevents the previous release from consuming unsupported entries or otherwise preserves their resumability across rollback.
findings.failure_scenario: An unowned land is queued or waiting for CI when deployment rolls back; the old daemon claims it and permanently blocks it instead of resuming it.

findings.title: Unowned lands are absent from the UI
findings.detail: The change creates no run for an unowned land, while the UI displays runs and has no land queue view or consumer of land entries. Consequently these entries cannot appear in the UI, despite the request requiring them to be shown there.
findings.suggestion: Add a UI view or equivalent presentation that reads land entries independently of runs and identifies entries with no owner.
findings.failure_scenario: A user queues an unowned PR and opens the dashboard: neither the queued entry nor its later blocked or landed state is visible.

structured.summary: Reviewed the land request, queue, persistence, CLI, feed and UI paths. The targeted store tests passed, but the land queue tests could not start because @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js is unavailable in this checkout.

findings.title: Unowned PRs cannot be requested by the documented PR number form
findings.detail: The existing CLI accepts a PR number, but the new unowned path accepts only a full GitHub URL. A number with no matching factory run is rejected as “run not found,” even when the PR exists on a configured repository.
findings.suggestion: Resolve supported PR references to an unambiguous configured repository and canonical URL before entering the unowned flow, or provide an explicit repository-qualified form.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless land 77 --sha <full-sha>` for an open unowned PR; the request is rejected before GitHub is queried.

findings.title: Rollback blocks active unowned lands
findings.detail: Unowned entries are persisted with an empty run ID. After a rollback, the previous release reads that value as a normal run ID; its land queue looks up the empty ID, throws “run  is gone,” and marks the entry blocked. An interrupted or queued land therefore cannot survive a rollback to the previous release.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-skew strategy that prevents the previous release from consuming unsupported entries or otherwise preserves their resumability across rollback.
findings.failure_scenario: An unowned land is queued or waiting for CI when deployment rolls back; the old daemon claims it and permanently blocks it instead of resuming it.

findings.title: Unowned lands are absent from the UI
findings.detail: The change creates no run for an unowned land, while the UI displays runs and has no land queue view or consumer of land entries. Consequently these entries cannot appear in the UI, despite the request requiring them to be shown there.
findings.suggestion: Add a UI view or equivalent presentation that reads land entries independently of runs and identifies entries with no owner.
findings.failure_scenario: A user queues an unowned PR and opens the dashboard: neither the queued entry nor its later blocked or landed state is visible.

Reviewed cleanup persistence, recovery, and run resumption. The focused test command passed 8 cases; 3 integration cases could not run because @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js was unavailable.

Reviewed cleanup persistence, recovery, and identity checks. The targeted test command passed eight process-level cases; three integration cases could not run because the MCP SDK module was unavailable in the environment.

findings.title: Recovery loses descendants that have not yet been recorded
findings.detail: The durable record contains only members discovered so far, and recovery kills only those rows before deleting them. The live sweep deliberately rescans after freezing because a descendant can fork between discovery and the freeze. If the daemon dies before that rescan, the new descendant has no row, remains running, and the resumed run proceeds after deleting the recorded members. A crash during initial discovery has the same problem for members later in the snapshot.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation-level ownership information before cleanup begins to rediscover marked descendants during recovery, and keep recovery unresolved until the full set has been swept and confirmed gone.
findings.failure_scenario: A marked process forks after the initial process snapshot but before SIGSTOP reaches it. The daemon dies after freezing the recorded parent and before the next scan. Startup kills the recorded parent, deletes the invocation's rows, and leaves the unrecorded child running in the checkout while the run resumes.

findings.title: Recovery misses descendants created during the freeze sweep
findings.detail: Recovery only visits PIDs already recorded. A marked process can fork after the initial discovery snapshot but before it receives SIGSTOP. If the daemon crashes after the stop and before the next discovery sweep records the new child, recovery kills the recorded parent, deletes the invocation's records, and leaves the child running. The resumed invocation can then enter the same checkout while that child still writes to it.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation discovery information to resume the sweep, and do not clear the cleanup until both recorded members and any descendants discovered after the crash are accounted for.
findings.failure_scenario: A marked parent forks between the snapshot at line 377 and its SIGSTOP; the daemon dies before the next snapshot, leaving the unrecorded child alive.

findings.title: Linux birth identities can match unrelated processes after reboot
findings.detail: On Linux, the persisted birth value is /proc's start time in ticks since boot. It does not identify the boot. If a machine reboots with cleanup records pending, a new unrelated process can have both the recorded PID and the same boot-relative start tick. Recovery will treat it as the old member and send SIGKILL.
findings.suggestion: Include a boot identity in persisted Linux process identities and refuse to signal a record from a different or unconfirmable boot.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending cleanup survives a reboot, and an unrelated process receives the same PID and start tick during the new boot.

Reviewed cleanup persistence, recovery and run startup. The targeted process-cleanup test had 8 passes; 3 tests could not run because the MCP SDK client module was unavailable in the environment.

Reviewed the cleanup persistence and recovery paths. The focused test command passed eight tests; three startup tests could not run because the checkout lacks the @modelcontextprotocol/sdk dependency.

findings.title: A crash during discovery leaves unrecorded descendants running
findings.detail: Members are persisted one at a time only after discovery begins, and recovery scans only persisted members. If the daemon dies before the loop records every discovered PID, the remaining marked descendants have no durable ownership record. Recovery deletes the partial record and permits the next invocation while those descendants continue running. The same gap exists for descendants created between the freeze and the subsequent rescan.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation ownership information before cleanup starts to rediscover and finish the complete marked set after a crash, and keep recovery unresolved until discovery and termination are confirmed complete.
findings.failure_scenario: An invocation has two marked sleepers. The daemon dies after recording the first PID but before recording the second. Restart recovery kills the first, deletes the invocation record, and leaves the second sleeper running in the checkout.

findings.title: Linux birth identities can match an unrelated process after reboot
findings.detail: On Linux, processBirth returns only the boot-relative start tick. Persisted records survive a reboot, but both PIDs and start ticks can be reused on the next boot. Recovery can therefore treat an unrelated process as the recorded member and send it SIGKILL.
findings.suggestion: Include a boot identity in the persisted Linux birth identity and require it to match before signalling.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending cleanup survives a reboot; a new process receives the recorded PID and starts at the same boot-relative tick. Daemon startup sends SIGKILL to that unrelated process.

findings.title: Checkout blocking compares command directories rather than checkout identity
findings.detail: The cross-run recovery filter requires exact cwd equality. Records store the individual command's cwd, which can be a subdirectory of the checkout, while run startup supplies the worktree root. If recovery fails for a record belonging to another run, a new run using the same checkout can miss that unresolved cleanup and proceed.
findings.suggestion: Persist and compare a canonical checkout identity independently of the command's working directory.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending cleanup from run A has cwd /checkout/subdir and cannot be confirmed. Run B resumes in /checkout and launches a command there; neither its run ID nor its cwd equals the record, so it starts despite the unresolved cleanup.

findings.title: A crash while recording the claimed set leaves unrecorded descendants running
findings.detail: Members are persisted one at a time, but recovery only examines persisted members and never rediscovers the invocation's other marked processes. A daemon crash between two writes leaves the remaining members absent from the record; if it crashes before the first write, there is no record at all. Recovery can therefore delete the partial record and allow the resumed invocation to start while a previous descendant still runs in the checkout.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation ownership information before cleanup begins to rediscover and finish the complete marked set after a crash, including crashes during the initial scan and later sweeps.
findings.failure_scenario: A cleanup scan finds two live descendants. The daemon dies after recording the first PID but before recording the second. Startup kills the first, deletes the invocation record, and resumes work while the second continues writing to the checkout.

findings.title: Linux birth identities can match unrelated processes after a reboot
findings.detail: Linux processBirth returns only the boot-relative start tick. Persisting that value across daemon restarts also persists it across machine reboots, when both PIDs and start ticks are reused. A process started at the same tick with the same PID after reboot will pass this comparison and receive SIGKILL even though it is unrelated to the recorded invocation.
findings.suggestion: Include a boot identity in the persisted Linux birth identity and verify it during recovery before signalling.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending record survives a reboot. An unrelated process receives the recorded PID and starts at the same boot-relative tick; daemon startup treats it as the old member and kills it.

findings.title: Timeout cleanup leaves detached test children running
findings.detail: The final kill targets only the timeout process group. Descendants that start a new session or process group are outside it and survive both the TERM and KILL. The existing subprocess utility starts commands with detached: true, so this is relevant to the suite. A surviving child can also keep inherited output pipes open and prevent the step from finishing, defeating log preservation. The added test exercises only children in the original group.
findings.suggestion: Track and stop descendants across process groups, and cover a detached child in the timeout test.
findings.failure_scenario: A hanging test has started a detached subprocess when the 20-minute limit expires; the wrapper exits while that subprocess remains alive.

findings.title: The inner timeout is measured from the step, not the job
findings.detail: The 20-minute timer starts only after checkout, Bun setup, installation, and Git configuration, while the 25-minute limit starts with the job. If those earlier steps take more than about four and a half minutes, the outer job timeout can cancel the job before the helper finishes its 30-second grace period, reproducing the missing-log failure this change is intended to prevent.
findings.suggestion: Base the check deadline on elapsed job time or otherwise ensure the inner timeout and grace period expire before the job deadline.
findings.failure_scenario: Setup and installation take five minutes, then the test suite hangs; the 25-minute job timeout arrives before the helper can emit and finish preserving its diagnostics.

findings.title: Detached descendants survive the timeout cleanup
findings.detail: The final cleanup kills only the timeout process group. A test or subprocess that starts a new session or process group is outside that group and survives both signals. The repository has tests and subprocess code that use detached processes. If such a process retains the step's output descriptors, the runner can continue waiting for output to close, defeating the goal of finishing the step before the job timeout.
findings.suggestion: Track and terminate the check's descendants across process groups, and add a timeout test with a detached child that inherits the output descriptors.
findings.failure_scenario: A hung test starts a detached child that holds stdout or stderr open. The wrapper reaches its deadline and kills its own group, but the detached child remains alive and keeps the step's log pipe open.

findings.title: The inner deadline is measured from the check step, not the job start
findings.detail: The 25-minute job timeout also includes checkout, Bun setup, installation, and Git configuration. If those steps take five minutes or more, a hung check is cancelled by the outer timeout before its 20-minute timer fires; with slightly less setup time, the tree dump and 30-second grace period may be cut off. That reproduces the missing-log failure this change is intended to prevent.
findings.suggestion: Set the inner deadline using the remaining job budget, or reserve sufficient time for preceding steps and the diagnostic grace period.
findings.failure_scenario: Dependency installation and setup take six minutes, then the test suite hangs. The job is cancelled after 19 minutes of the check, before the wrapper prints the process tree.

output.summary:
Reviewed the audit, feedback, and publication paths. Targeted tests could not run because dependencies are absent: `bun test test/gates.test.ts test/git-integrity.test.ts test/pipeline-audit.test.ts` failed with `Cannot find package 'entities'`.

Reviewed the audit and publication paths. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency; Bun reported “Cannot find package 'entities'” for all three test files.

findings.title: Advisory warnings do not give the implementer a chance to remove scratch files
findings.detail: The new warnings are appended only when another implement stage already occurs. Because warnings do not produce audit feedback that triggers another round, an otherwise passing change proceeds through review and publication without the implementer seeing them. The added approve-case test confirms that only one implement prompt occurs. This leaves the reported failure mode in place when the scratch output is the only problem.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for the implementer to receive the advisory and have an opportunity to remove accidental output before publication, while keeping intentional additions non-blocking.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer adds `.tmp-gate/report.xml`, gates pass, and the reviewer approves. The audit records a warning, but no subsequent implement prompt is sent; the scratch file remains in the published history.

findings.title: Diagnose decoding failures in filenames as well as patch bodies
findings.detail: The aggregate publication scan includes raw diff headers, but diagnosis only checks patch sections that have an index line. A decoding-limit failure caused by a pathname can occur in the raw header or in a mode-only patch without an index line, so diagnosis falls through and rethrows the original generic “Published content” error without the commit or path.
findings.suggestion: Inspect each raw diff entry’s path for decoding failures and associate it with the revision before inspecting its patch body.
findings.failure_scenario: A commit adds a file whose name contains a repeatedly percent-encoded sequence that exceeds the decoding limit. The aggregate scan refuses publication, but the diagnosis cannot reliably attribute the raw-header failure and can return the generic refusal without the requested commit and path.

findings.title: Encoded credentials can escape through the new path diagnostic
findings.detail: The new diagnostic passes the raw Git path to redactCredentials, which replaces only literal credential variants. A percent-encoded credential in a filename therefore survives redaction and can leave the process in the publication error. The audit's new filename feedback has the same risk. Previously, the publication refusal did not include the path.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported encodings before credential redaction, or suppress the path when its decoded forms contain a registered credential. Apply the same protection to audit filenames.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential is encoded into a filename, and that file contains text that exceeds the private decoding limit. The resulting publication refusal includes the encoded credential in its path.

findings.title: Attribute decoding failures by path, not only by blob IDs
findings.detail: The diagnosis finds a file’s raw record by matching its old and new blob IDs. Multiple files can have the same pair of IDs, so it can report the first file even when the decoding failure occurs in another file’s pathname. This gives the owner the wrong cause of the publication refusal.
findings.suggestion: Associate each patch section with its corresponding raw record by position or by parsing its path, rather than assuming blob ID pairs are unique.
findings.failure_scenario: A commit adds a.txt and a second file whose name contains an over-encoded sequence, both with identical contents. The second pathname triggers the decoding refusal, but both additions have the same blob IDs and the diagnostic names a.txt.

findings.title: Include large text logs containing terminal control characters
findings.detail: The size map excludes any blob that fails reviewableText, which rejects ESC and other control bytes even when Git treats the file as text. Gate output commonly contains ANSI color escapes, so a large new log can evade the requested large-text warning.
findings.suggestion: Determine eligibility for the size warning using the text classification used for the diff, rather than requiring the stricter executable-content reviewability check.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer commits a 150 KiB text log outside a root hidden directory containing ANSI color sequences. It receives neither the large-text warning nor the hidden-directory warning.

The publication scan does not include registered credentials, and URL-safe base64 bypasses the new decoder. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency.

findings.title: Publication checks do not include registered credentials
findings.detail: The new decoder only checks entries supplied by its caller. Production publication paths supply private-string entries, while registered credentials are included only in the separate filename diagnosis. Literal credential redaction does not remove a base64 encoding, so encoded credentials can still be published in PR text or commit content. The new publication test constructs a combined list itself and therefore does not exercise the production wiring.
findings.suggestion: Include registered credentials in the protected values used by every publication content check, and test through a production caller.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential absent from private-strings.txt appears as base64 in a PR body or changed file; publication checks receive no matching entry and allow it.

findings.title: Base64 decoding cannot expose another encoded layer
findings.detail: A base64 run is decoded only if its immediate decoded bytes already contain the protected value. Thus base64 of a percent-encoded or HTML-encoded value never reaches the subsequent decoding passes, and the encoded filename or content is allowed. The targeted command `bun -e 'import {privateMatches} from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const s="synthetic-secret-credential"; const p=Array.from(s,c=>`%${c.charCodeAt(0).toString(16)}`).join(""); console.log(JSON.stringify(privateMatches(Buffer.from(p).toString("base64"),[{value:s,entry:1}])));'` printed `[]`.
findings.suggestion: Check candidate base64 decodings through the supported subsequent decoding layers before deciding whether to retain them, with bounded recursion and tests for combined encodings.
findings.failure_scenario: A filename contains base64 of the percent-encoded registered credential; audit findings retain the encoded filename and diagnostic instead of redacting them.

findings.title: Include registered credentials in publication scans
findings.detail: The new base64 matching only checks the entries supplied by callers. Production publication callers supply private-strings entries, not registered credentials; literal redaction before publication does not remove an encoded credential. The added publication test constructs a combined list itself, so it does not exercise the production boundary.
findings.suggestion: Include registered credentials in the protected entries used for publication text and repository content checks, and test through a production caller.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR body, commit, or published file contains the base64 encoding of a registered credential that is absent from private-strings.txt. The scan accepts it and the encoded credential can be published.

findings.title: Recognize URL-safe base64 encodings
findings.detail: The base64 run expression excludes '-' and '_', so URL-safe encodings are split before decoding. The same bypass affects publication checks and audit filename redaction. A focused check returned no matches: `bun -e 'import {privateMatches} from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const value="synthetic-secret-???"; const encoded=Buffer.from(value).toString("base64url"); console.log(JSON.stringify({encoded,matches:privateMatches(encoded,[{value,entry:1}])}));'` produced `{"encoded":"c3ludGhldGljLXNlY3JldC0_Pz8","matches":[]}`.
findings.suggestion: Recognize the URL-safe alphabet as well as standard base64 and cover it in publication and audit tests.
findings.failure_scenario: A filename or published text contains `c3ludGhldGljLXNlY3JldC0_Pz8`, the URL-safe base64 encoding of a protected value. It is retained instead of being redacted or blocked.

findings.failure_scenario: A filename or published text contains `c3ludGhldGljLXNlY3JldC0_Pz8`, the URL-safe base64 encoding of a protected value. It is retained instead of being redacted or blocked.

findings.title: Include registered credentials in publication checks
findings.detail: Publication checks match only the entries supplied by their callers. Production callers supply private-strings entries, not registered credentials, so the new base64 decoder never checks credentials in outgoing content, commit messages, or PR text. The new unit test constructs a combined list manually, unlike those production paths. A standalone check with an empty production-style entry list returned no match: `bun -e 'import { privateMatches } from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const v="secret-token-123"; const s=Buffer.from(v).toString("base64"); console.log(JSON.stringify({encoded:s,actual:privateMatches(s,[])}));'` printed `{"encoded":"c2VjcmV0LXRva2VuLTEyMw==","actual":[]}`.
findings.suggestion: Include registered credentials in the protected values used by every publication entry point, and test through a production caller.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential is base64-encoded in a file being published, while it is absent from private-strings.txt; the publication check permits it.

findings.title: Decode nested encodings before deciding whether base64 matches
findings.detail: A base64 run is replaced only when its immediate decoded text already contains a protected value. Consequently, a base64-encoded percent encoding or a twice-base64-encoded value never reaches the subsequent decoding rounds. The direct check `bun -e 'import { privateMatches } from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const v="secret-token-123"; for (const s of [Buffer.from(Buffer.from(v).toString("base64")).toString("base64"), Buffer.from([...v].map(c=>"%"+c.charCodeAt(0).toString(16)).join("")).toString("base64")]) console.log(s, JSON.stringify(privateMatches(s,[{value:v,entry:1}])));'` returned `[]` for both inputs. The same decoder is used for audit filenames and publication content.
findings.suggestion: Check eligible base64 candidates through the bounded decoding layers before deciding they are unrelated, while preserving the decoding limit and false-positive controls.
findings.failure_scenario: A filename contains the base64 encoding of a percent-encoded registered credential; its audit finding retains the filename and detail instead of withholding them.

findings.title: Layered base64 encoding bypasses protected-text matching
findings.detail: A base64 run is decoded only when its first decoded form already contains a protected value. Consequently, base64 wrapping another supported encoding never reaches the successive decoding rounds. Both publication checks and audit filename checks can let the encoded secret through. The direct probe `bun -e 'import {privateMatches} from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const value="synthetic-secret"; const encoded=Buffer.from(value).toString("base64"); const double=Buffer.from(encoded).toString("base64"); console.log({encoded,double,result:privateMatches(double,[{value,entry:1}])});'` returned `result: []` for `YzNsdWRHaGxkR2xqTFhObFkzSmxkQT09`.
findings.suggestion: Check eligible base64 candidates through the bounded decoding layers before deciding whether to retain a decoded form, and cover layered base64 and percent encodings in publication and audit tests.
findings.failure_scenario: A filename or published text contains the base64 encoding of the base64 or percent-encoded form of a registered credential. The matching check returns no hit, allowing that encoded credential to be persisted or published.

output.summary:
Reviewed the statistics aggregation, eval recording paths, CLI and HTTP integration. The workload unit tests passed. The targeted CLI and HTTP tests could not be validated in this checkout: the installed Zod lacks prefault, and the MCP SDK client module is missing.

Reviewed the aggregation, eval runner, CLI and HTTP paths. The workload test file passed. The CLI and HTTP tests could not run reliably because installed dependencies are missing or mismatched: the MCP SDK module was missing and the installed Zod lacks prefault.

findings.title: Eval trial totals are attributed to a single provider even when several providers were called
findings.detail: The eval runner can combine calls to finders and verifiers from different providers into one trial result. This code assigns the entire trial's cost and tokens to details.provider and counts it as one invocation. Consequently, the other providers disappear from the eval workload and the selected provider receives their usage.
findings.suggestion: Use per-call provider evidence where it is available; where the stored trial cannot distinguish calls, avoid presenting the combined usage as a single provider's measured workload.
findings.failure_scenario: A review eval uses provider A for its primary call and provider B for a verifier. The reported eval statistics assign both calls' tokens and cost to A, report one invocation, and omit B.

findings.title: Discard available cached-token totals for implementation evals
findings.detail: Every implementation eval with round evidence takes the null branch, even though the runner records cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens on the trial. A single such trial makes the provider's aggregate cache and input token totals null, including when it has only one round and the split is fully attributable.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the stored trial-level cache totals wherever they can be attributed, including single-round trials and aggregate totals.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation eval has one round with 100 input tokens, 30 cache-read tokens and 10 cache-write tokens. Its eval statistics report all three split metrics as unknown.

findings.title: Count grading failures as unsuccessful provider invocations
findings.detail: For implementation evals, the runner can overwrite roundEvidence.status with an error or timeout from grading after the provider invocation succeeded. Using that field as the invocation status therefore reports provider success rates based partly on local grading outcomes.
findings.suggestion: Use persisted invocation-status evidence for the success share, or mark the status unknown where the persisted round does not distinguish invocation and grading outcomes.
findings.failure_scenario: A provider returns successfully but the implementation grader times out. The round is counted as an unsuccessful provider invocation.

findings.title: Existing UI requests now load and process all historical eval output
findings.detail: The existing provider workload endpoint is used by several UI pages. Each request now synchronously reads every matching invocation and SELECTs every column of every eval trial, including potentially large output and details JSON, then repeatedly filters and sorts the records. With the default unbounded window, cost and memory grow with the entire database and can block the daemon when an existing page requests its former lightweight seven-day statistics.
findings.suggestion: Keep the existing lightweight workload path for existing callers and aggregate historical statistics without loading unneeded trial output or repeatedly scanning all records.
findings.failure_scenario: After a long-running installation accumulates many eval trials with large outputs, opening the Providers, Models or Setup page loads and parses all historical trials on the daemon's request path.

findings.title: Panel and sampled eval calls are attributed to one trial target
findings.detail: The fallback treats an entire eval trial as one provider invocation. Review panels and sampled reviews can make several provider calls, including calls to other providers and models; the runner combines their token and cost totals into the trial. This code assigns all of that work to the trial's target and reports one execution, so provider and model workload totals are wrong.
findings.suggestion: Use per-call evidence where available and represent attribution that cannot be recovered as unknown rather than charging the combined trial to one provider.
findings.failure_scenario: A review panel calls provider A for its finder and provider B for verification. The reported eval workload charges both calls' tokens and cost to A, counts one execution, and omits B's work.

findings.title: Recorded eval cache usage is discarded for every implementation round
findings.detail: Whenever a trial has rounds, cache-read and cache-write are forced to null even though the runner persists their totals on the trial. A normal single-round implementation eval therefore loses measurements that are available, and one such row makes the corresponding aggregate null.
findings.suggestion: Use the trial's recorded cache split when it can be attributed to the selected round or group, including single-round trials.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation trial with one recorded round and cacheReadTokens of 100 reports unknown cache-read tokens and unknown uncached input for its provider, model, role and day.

Reviewed the aggregation, CLI and HTTP paths, and eval recording. The database workload tests passed. Reviewed the aggregation, CLI and HTTP paths against invocation and eval persistence. The provider-workload tests passed. CLI and HTTP tests could not be verified because the installed dependencies are incomplete or incompatible: the HTTP test could not resolve @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js, and the CLI tests failed during startup because floors.prefault is unavailable.

findings.title: Attribute panel and retry calls as separate provider work
findings.detail: An eval trial or round can contain multiple harness calls. The runner combines panel finder and verifier results, and can combine a failed resume attempt with its retry, into the trial or round totals. This code counts that combined record once and attributes all of its tokens and cost to the trial's target provider and model. Consequently, panel members on other providers disappear from the workload, and invocation counts and per-provider costs are wrong.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individually recorded call evidence where available, and represent cases without sufficient attribution as unknown rather than assigning the combined work to one provider.
findings.failure_scenario: A review eval calls a finder on provider A and a verifier on provider B. The output reports one invocation and the combined spend under A, with no invocation or spend under B.

findings.title: Preserve known cache metrics for single-round evals
findings.detail: Every eval with round evidence has its cache read and write metrics forced to null, even when there is only one round and the trial records both cache totals. Implement evals normally record rounds, so their known input and cached-token statistics are lost. A single such record also makes the corresponding provider aggregate null.
findings.suggestion: Use the trial's cache totals when they can be attributed unambiguously, including the single-round case.
findings.failure_scenario: A one-round implement eval records 100 total input tokens, 20 cache-read tokens, and 10 cache-write tokens. Its workload reports inputTokens, cacheReadTokens, and cacheWriteTokens as null instead of 70, 20, and 10.

findings.title: Do not filter every eval round by the first round's start time
findings.detail: The cutoff is applied to the trial's creation time before its rounds are expanded. The runner sets that time at the first round, so later rounds are excluded when they run after the requested cutoff. Their day is likewise assigned to the first round's day.
findings.suggestion: Record or use per-round timestamps for filtering and day attribution; where historical records lack them, expose that limitation instead of presenting the first round's timestamp as each call's time.
findings.failure_scenario: An implement trial starts before midnight and retries after midnight. A `--since` cutoff at midnight omits the retry entirely, and an unfiltered report assigns it to the previous day.

findings.title: Panel eval spend is attributed to the trial target
findings.detail: A review eval can invoke finders and verifiers on other providers and models. The runner combines their usage and cost into the trial result, but this code attributes the entire trial to details.provider and t.model_id. The resulting provider and model workload totals are wrong for both the target and the other panel members.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individually attributed invocation evidence where available, and represent unattributable panel usage explicitly instead of assigning it to the trial target.
findings.failure_scenario: A review trial targeting provider A invokes a verifier on provider B. B's tokens and cost appear under A, while B has no corresponding eval workload.

findings.title: Implement evals lose their recorded input and cache token totals
findings.detail: Every implement eval with recorded rounds sets both cache token fields to null, even though the runner records aggregate cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens on the trial. Since summarize propagates any null, one such eval makes the provider's entire input and cached-token totals unknown, including for a single-round trial where attribution is unambiguous.
findings.suggestion: Use the trial's recorded cache totals when they can be attributed to the same provider and model, and preserve explicitly unknown splits only when attribution is genuinely ambiguous.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-round implement eval records 100 input tokens, including 20 cache-read tokens and 10 cache-write tokens. Its provider's eval totals report inputTokens, cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens as null.

findings.title: Eval success share uses grading failures as invocation failures
findings.detail: For implement rounds, the runner changes roundEvidence.status to error or timeout when grading fails, even if the provider invocation returned ok. Counting that status as the invocation result understates provider success and makes the metric depend on local grading rather than provider calls.
findings.suggestion: Use separately persisted invocation status for the success metric, or mark it unknown when the stored round does not distinguish invocation and grading outcomes.
findings.failure_scenario: A model invocation returns ok, but its implementation grading times out. The eval workload reports a zero successful share for that invocation.

output.summary:
The classifier and rerun paths were reviewed. The targeted test command could not run because the checkout is missing the entities package.

Reviewed signature selection, excerpt construction, rerun compatibility, and credential redaction. Targeted tests could not load because the checkout is missing the entities dependency; a direct Bun probe reproduced an excerpt boundary defect.

findings.title: Preserve exact-value redaction for short image credentials
findings.detail: The publication window includes surrounding log text when calling redactCredentials. Credentials shorter than eight characters are redacted only when the entire input equals the credential, so an Image value that previously matched exactly now remains in the image field and serialized signature. Those values can be persisted and sent in CI evidence.
findings.suggestion: Preserve exact-value redaction for the selected field while retaining surrounding context for credentials that cross the window boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: With registered credential `abc123` and log `Image: abc123\n(fail) example`, `bun -e` calling ciSignature returns `image: "abc123"` and signature `["test","(fail) example","abc123"]`; the previous implementation redacted the image value.

findings.title: Long failing lines lose their test name from the excerpt
findings.detail: When an assertion is followed by a `(fail)` line longer than the remaining excerpt budget, the tail window keeps only the end of that line. The signature names the failure, but the excerpt omits both `(fail)` and the test name. A direct probe returned `{"line":"(fail) important test xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx","excerptHasName":false,"excerptLength":1999}` for the command in the failure scenario.
findings.suggestion: Reserve space for the beginning of the selected signature line before filling the remaining excerpt with preceding diagnostic context.
findings.failure_scenario: Run `bun -e 'import {ciSignature} from "./src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts"; const r=ciSignature("test", "error: assertion\n" + "context\n".repeat(200) + "(fail) important test " + "x".repeat(3000), "fallback"); console.log(JSON.stringify({line:r.line.slice(0,40), excerptHasName:r.excerpt.includes("important test"), excerptLength:r.excerpt.length}));'`. The selected signature starts with `(fail) important test`, but the excerpt does not contain the name.

findings.title: A rejected event batch aborts the signal needed to report failure
findings.detail: A rejected events request aborts the agent job controller. The catch block then skips the failure POST because jobSignal is already aborted. The coordinator continues to see the job as leased until its lease expires, and records a lease-expiry reason instead of the event-delivery failure. This violates the requirement that a rejected batch fail the job.
findings.suggestion: Keep event-delivery failure distinct from cancellation and report it using a bounded signal that remains usable after stopping the harness.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator returns HTTP 400 for an oversized or invalid events batch while the harness is running. The harness is aborted, but no failure is posted and the job remains leased until expiry.

findings.title: Periodic fencing can let a partitioned agent run past its lease
findings.detail: The fence checks only once per heartbeat interval and uses a strict greater-than comparison. With the default 60-second lease and 10-second interval, a check at or just before the deadline does nothing, and the next check can occur nearly 10 seconds later. During that interval the coordinator can expire the lease while the worker continues running the agent and spending quota.
findings.suggestion: Schedule fencing against the actual heartbeat deadline and reset that deadline after each successful heartbeat, aborting as soon as the lease period expires.
findings.failure_scenario: Heartbeat requests fail immediately after a successful heartbeat. At 60 seconds the coordinator may expire the lease, but the worker can continue the harness until the next periodic fence check around 70 seconds.

findings.title: A rejected event batch aborts the job without reporting failure
findings.detail: The batch rejection handler aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure request because `jobSignal.aborted` is true. The coordinator retains the job as leased until its lease expires, instead of immediately failing the attempt.
findings.suggestion: Track event-post failures separately from cancellation, abort the harness, and report the failure using a signal that remains usable for the failure request.
findings.failure_scenario: An events request is rejected with HTTP 400 or 413 while the worker still holds the lease. The harness stops, but no failure is posted and the job remains leased until expiry.

findings.title: Event sequence numbers restart on a retried job
findings.detail: Each worker attempt starts `seq` at zero, while the coordinator retains events by job ID and ignores conflicts on `(job_id, seq)`. If an attempt posts events and then fails, the next attempt's batches collide with the earlier ones and are silently discarded; later batches can also mix output from different attempts.
findings.suggestion: Make event identity attempt-aware or establish a coordinator-managed sequence and clear retry semantics before reporting events.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts batch 0 and fails. Worker B retries the same job, posts its own batch 0, and completes. The coordinator keeps A's batch and discards B's batch, so the completed job has incorrect event history.

findings.title: Periodic fencing can let an agent run beyond its lease period
findings.detail: The fence checks only once per heartbeat interval and uses a strict greater-than comparison. With the default 60-second lease and 10-second heartbeat interval, an agent can continue for nearly 70 seconds after the last successful heartbeat, after the coordinator is entitled to expire and reassign the lease.
findings.suggestion: Arm or reset a deadline timer on each successful heartbeat so running agents are aborted when the lease period expires.
findings.failure_scenario: Heartbeats fail immediately after a successful heartbeat. The coordinator expires the lease at 60 seconds, but the next worker fence check can occur almost 10 seconds later, allowing overlapping attempts and extra model spending.

findings.detail: The batch rejection handler aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure request because `jobSignal.aborted` is true. The coordinator retains the job as leased until its lease expires, instead of immediately failing the attempt.
findings.suggestion: Track event-post failures separately from cancellation, abort the harness, and report the failure using a signal that remains usable for the failure request.
findings.failure_scenario: An events request is rejected with HTTP 400 or 413 while the worker still holds the lease. The harness stops, but no failure is posted and the job remains leased until expiry.

findings.title: Event sequence numbers restart on a retried job
findings.detail: Each worker attempt starts `seq` at zero, while the coordinator retains events by job ID and ignores conflicts on `(job_id, seq)`. If an attempt posts events and then fails, the next attempt's batches collide with the earlier ones and are silently discarded; later batches can also mix output from different attempts.
findings.suggestion: Make event identity attempt-aware or establish a coordinator-managed sequence and clear retry semantics before reporting events.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts batch 0 and fails. Worker B retries the same job, posts its own batch 0, and completes. The coordinator keeps A's batch and discards B's batch, so the completed job has incorrect event history.

findings.title: Periodic fencing can let an agent run beyond its lease period
findings.detail: The fence checks only once per heartbeat interval and uses a strict greater-than comparison. With the default 60-second lease and 10-second heartbeat interval, an agent can continue for nearly 70 seconds after the last successful heartbeat, after the coordinator is entitled to expire and reassign the lease.
findings.suggestion: Arm or reset a deadline timer on each successful heartbeat so running agents are aborted when the lease period expires.
findings.failure_scenario: Heartbeats fail immediately after a successful heartbeat. The coordinator expires the lease at 60 seconds, but the next worker fence check can occur almost 10 seconds later, allowing overlapping attempts and extra model spending.

findings.title: Retrying a job reuses event sequence numbers
findings.detail: Every worker attempt starts its sequence at zero, but the coordinator retains event batches across attempts and ignores inserts with an existing job ID and sequence. A later attempt can complete successfully while its early events are silently replaced by those from the failed attempt.
findings.suggestion: Make event identity attempt-aware, or clear or otherwise reconcile prior attempt batches when a job is retried.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts sequence 0 and disconnects. Worker B leases the same job, posts its own sequence 0, and completes; the coordinator returns success for the post but retains worker A's batch.

findings.title: A rejected event batch does not report job failure
findings.detail: A rejected post aborts the job controller. The catch handler then skips the failure endpoint because the job signal is aborted, so the coordinator continues to hold the job until its lease expires instead of receiving the required failure report. The existing rejection test only checks that no result is posted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish event-post failures from cancellation and report the failure using a still-live bounded signal before ending the attempt.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator rejects an events batch with HTTP 400 while the lease remains valid; the harness is aborted, but no failure request is sent and the job remains leased until expiry.

findings.title: Fencing can occur a heartbeat interval after lease expiry
findings.detail: The periodic fence checks only every heartbeat interval and uses a strict greater-than comparison. An agent can continue running and spending quota for nearly another interval after the last successful heartbeat exceeds one lease period. A job can also start while the heartbeat is already stale and run until the next check.
findings.suggestion: Schedule fencing against the actual last-success deadline and refuse or immediately abort newly leased jobs while that deadline has passed.
findings.failure_scenario: With the default 60-second lease and 10-second heartbeat interval, a partition just after a successful heartbeat can leave an agent running until approximately 70 seconds after that heartbeat.

findings.title: Event sequence numbers collide across job attempts
findings.detail: Each attempt starts its sequence at zero, but the coordinator retains event rows when it requeues a failed agent job and ignores inserts that conflict on job ID and sequence. A later attempt can therefore finish successfully while its initial event batches are silently discarded and the previous attempt's events remain.
findings.suggestion: Make event identity and ordering account for the attempt, or arrange for a new attempt to use a coordinator-provided sequence that cannot collide with retained rows.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts sequence 0, then fails or loses its lease. Worker B leases the same job, posts its own sequence 0, and completes; the coordinator keeps worker A's batch and discards worker B's batch.

findings.title: A rejected event batch is not reported as a job failure
findings.detail: A rejected post aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure endpoint because the job signal is already aborted. The coordinator continues to hold the job until its lease expires, with no failure reason from the worker.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a batch rejection from cancellation and fencing, abort the harness, and report the failure using a signal that remains usable for the failure notification.
findings.failure_scenario: The events endpoint returns 400 for an oversized batch while the lease is valid. The harness is aborted, but the job remains leased until expiry instead of being promptly failed or requeued.

findings.title: Periodic fencing can run well after the lease period
findings.detail: The fence checks only every heartbeat interval. With the production 60-second lease and 10-second interval, a heartbeat that succeeds just after a check can leave a partitioned agent running for almost 70 seconds after its last successful heartbeat. The coordinator may have expired and reassigned the lease while the original harness continues spending quota.
findings.suggestion: Schedule a deadline from each successful heartbeat and abort at that deadline, resetting it after each subsequent success.
findings.failure_scenario: A heartbeat succeeds immediately after a fence tick and subsequent heartbeats fail. The tick just before 60 seconds does nothing, and the agent keeps running until the following tick.

findings.title: Keep local panel finders off workers explicitly
findings.detail: Every production review call receives checkout metadata, including calls from finders configured with local: true. The executor has no local-finder flag; it excludes only targets with backend, openai, or decisions fields. A free Claude or Codex CLI provider can have none of those fields, so its local finder is dispatched to a worker. This violates the requirement that local finders stay local and can also consume worker capacity intended for production reviews.
findings.suggestion: Carry the finder’s local designation into the call and omit checkout metadata or otherwise make that call ineligible for worker dispatch. Add coverage using a free CLI target without backend metadata.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel has a finder with local: true, routing selects a configured free claude-cli provider without a backend URL, and workers.agents includes review for the repository. The finder creates a worker job instead of running locally.

findings.title: Local panel finders can be dispatched to workers
findings.detail: Eligibility does not carry or check the finder's `local` flag. The engine expresses that flag only as a `free_only` routing constraint, which does not guarantee that the selected target has a backend, OpenAI, or decisions field. A free provider using a plain Claude or Codex CLI therefore passes this eligibility check. An explicitly selected review model can also bypass the billing filter. The finder is sent to a worker even though the request requires local finders to remain local.
findings.suggestion: Carry the local-finder distinction through the invocation seam and exclude those calls explicitly from worker eligibility; cover it with a panel test using an otherwise eligible CLI target.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel has a finder marked `local: true`, workers are enabled for review, and routing selects a free Claude CLI provider without backend fields. The finder creates a worker job instead of running on the coordinator.
