findings.title: The command cannot run against this checkout’s dataset
findings.detail: The generator unconditionally reads the default implement case file, but this commit contains no evals/implement directory or cases.json. The documented command therefore fails before querying any PR or creating a case. The tests supply a separate synthetic casePath and do not exercise the CLI’s default path.
findings.suggestion: Provide the required dataset at the default path or support initializing it in a way compatible with the runner and ID sequence.
findings.failure_scenario: In a fresh checkout of this commit, running the documented generator command attempts to read evals/implement/cases.json and fails with ENOENT.

findings.title: Accepted cases can be rejected by the eval runner as contaminated
findings.detail: Generated cases omit snapshot mode and validation never applies the runner’s history-contamination check. The runner rejects implement pins whose reachable history contains evals/implement, even if the hidden command passed at base and head. Consequently, PRs merged after the dataset appeared can be reported as accepted but cannot be run as implement evals.
findings.suggestion: Validate cases through the runner’s contamination rules and use an appropriate supported snapshot path or exclude incompatible pins with a clear reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR has a base commit descended from a commit touching evals/implement; its hidden tests fail at base and pass at head, so the generator accepts it, but every trial fails preparation with a pinned-history contamination error.

findings.title: The CLI never looks up available production complexity
findings.detail: Although generateReplayCases accepts an injected lookupRun, the actual CLI supplies no lookup. Thus every case generated by the requested command defaults to medium, including runs whose triage complexity is available in the local run store. This loses a required production signal and can give the eval an incorrect complexity.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only run-record lookup, retaining the documented fallback only when the record or complexity is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: A factory PR’s footer identifies a locally recorded run with complexity small; the documented command generates a medium case and notes that lookup was not configured.

findings.title: The CLI never retrieves production complexity
findings.detail: The documented generator does not supply `lookupRun`, so every CLI-generated case gets `medium` even when the local production run record contains its actual triage complexity. The injectable lookup exercised by tests is unavailable through the requested command, making the complexity requirement ineffective for normal use.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only production run lookup and retain the explicit unknown fallback only when the record or complexity is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR has a report footer naming a locally stored run whose triage complexity is `small`; running the documented command creates a case with complexity `medium`.

findings.title: Known large-complexity runs cannot become replay cases
findings.detail: The production complexity is passed directly into `ImplementCaseSchema`, which accepts only `trivial`, `small`, and `medium`. A run lookup returning `large` therefore excludes the PR before validation. This prevents generating cases for a class of harder production tasks the request seeks to capture.
findings.suggestion: Extend the implement case and runner contracts to support production complexity values, or establish an explicit compatible representation that preserves the recorded value.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR has valid hidden tests and a production run with `complexity: large`; the generator reports a schema error and omits it.

findings.title: Interrupted publication permanently blocks the next case ID
findings.detail: Hidden files are created before the case file is atomically replaced. If the process stops between those operations, the hidden directory remains without a corresponding case. On the next run the same ID is selected and the existing-directory check rejects it, so subsequent PRs also cannot be added without manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Stage hidden files under a temporary name and make interrupted publication recoverable on the next invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: The generator is interrupted after creating `hidden/impl-013` but before renaming the updated cases file; every later invocation selects `impl-013` and reports that its hidden destination already exists.

Reviewed snapshot creation, gate execution, reuse, and evidence handling. Targeted tests could not start because installed dependencies were incomplete or incompatible: Zod lacked overwrite and prefault, and the entities package was missing.

findings.title: Reuse can accept a result produced against different Git metadata
findings.detail: The snapshot checkout uses a synthetic commit with a different SHA, message, author, timestamp, and potentially parent relationship from the eventual round commit. Gate commands can inspect that metadata, but the reuse key compares only the tree and gate configuration and environment. A passing snapshot result can therefore suppress a test that would fail on the actual round commit, and can become verification evidence.
findings.suggestion: Either make the gate execution observe the actual round commit or prevent reuse when equivalence of the Git metadata visible to the check cannot be established.
findings.failure_scenario: A test check runs `git log -1 --format=%s | grep -q 'Factory gate snapshot'`. It passes in the snapshot checkout, but fails against the round commit; the gates stage reuses the pass without running it.

findings.title: In-session gate omits the normal timeout retry
findings.detail: The in-session path invokes regression retries but does not perform the gates stage's full rerun when all failed checks time out. Timed-out results are also excluded from the execution record, so the session immediately receives a failure and the gates stage runs the suite again instead of carrying over the gate's retry and classification.
findings.suggestion: Apply the normal gate timeout-retry behavior to the in-session execution and persist the completed result and its first attempt for reuse.
findings.failure_scenario: The test check times out on its first attempt and would pass on the normal timeout rerun. The wrapper reports failure without retrying, records no reusable result, and the gates stage starts the test check again.

findings.title: A failed confinement check can return a successful command status
findings.detail: The wrapper status is derived from the exit code without considering result.ok. The gate runner marks a result failed when its output indicates a confinement launch failure even if the process exits zero, so the session can receive exit status zero alongside a factory gate FAIL message.
findings.suggestion: Return a nonzero status whenever the gate result is not OK, including confinement failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate command emits the recognized sandbox launch-failure diagnostic and exits zero. The result is marked as a confinement failure, but the wrapper exits successfully.

findings.title: Do not cache a result if the gate changed the snapshot checkout
findings.detail: The snapshot execution records its result under the original tree hash without checking whether setup or the test command changed HEAD. The normal gates stage checks HEAD before accepting gate evidence. A setup command can check out another commit before the test runs, causing a passing result for that commit to be reused as evidence for the candidate tree.
findings.suggestion: Record the snapshot checkout's initial commit and verify that HEAD still identifies it after execution before storing reusable evidence.
findings.failure_scenario: The candidate tree contains a failing test, but gate setup checks out the passing base commit. The test passes there, and the result is recorded and reused for the candidate tree.

findings.title: Include the gate worker count in the environment identity
findings.detail: The key uses gateEnvDigest, which does not include LIMITLESS_TEST_WORKERS, even though gateEnv explicitly sets that variable from resolveTestWorkers and passes it to gate commands. A changed worker count therefore produces the same environment hash and can reuse a result obtained under different test concurrency.
findings.suggestion: Include LIMITLESS_TEST_WORKERS in the gate environment digest used for the execution key.
findings.failure_scenario: An in-session gate passes with one test worker, the configured worker count changes before the gates stage, and a concurrency-sensitive suite that would fail with multiple workers is reused as a pass.

Reviewed the in-place executor, lease, restart, retry, and release-change paths. The targeted executor test could not start because the checkout is missing the entities package: `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` reported `Cannot find package 'entities'`. The findings below are based on code inspection.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and process birth; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor stops making progress while its process remains alive, a leased job eventually fails its lease, but waitStopped continues waiting for that same live process to set stopped. The daemon cannot fall back or start another gate, and cancellation can wait indefinitely as well.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path when an executor stops responding.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process is suspended or its event loop stalls during a long check. Its lease expires, but its PID remains alive, so the daemon remains in waitStopped rather than completing the failure path.

findings.title: Restart cancels running targeted retries instead of reattaching
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. Targeted regression retries and timeout reruns are also submitted as in-place jobs, but a restart rejects their saved handles and cancels the running checks. This misses the requested restart behavior for targeted retries and can repeat a long-running command.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching in-place retry, and allow its purpose through the resume path.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a `regression-retry-targeted` job is running. On resume, the saved handle fails the purpose whitelist and the executor job is cancelled instead of attached.

findings.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not signal a release change
findings.detail: The executor detects release changes solely through this new setting. A rollback to the base release starts code that never updates `executor.daemonRelease`, leaving the newer release SHA in the database. The newer executor therefore continues its running job instead of stopping it, while the older daemon resumes using its in-process gate path.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator release identity that remains detectable across rollback to a release predating this setting, and stop or refuse old jobs before the older daemon can reuse their worktrees.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release executor is running a gate when deployment rolls back to the base release. The old daemon does not write the setting, so the executor sees no release change and its gate can overlap the old daemon's resumed gate.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is checked before either job is enqueued
findings.detail: The scan for existing worktree jobs and insertion of the new job are separate operations, with the insertion deferred until attach after the handle is saved. Two concurrent starts for the same cwd can both observe no job and subsequently enqueue. With multiple executor processes, both jobs can lease and run in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Make worktree ownership an atomic database claim that is acquired before starting or enqueueing a job and released only after its processes are confirmed stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: Two gate requests for the same cwd enter start concurrently before either reaches attach, and two executor processes lease the resulting rows.

findings.title: Rollback to an older daemon leaves the old executor running
findings.detail: Release-change detection depends entirely on the daemon writing executor.daemonRelease. A release predating this change never writes that setting, so after a rollback it retains the newer release SHA. The executor therefore continues renewing and running its jobs while the older daemon resumes the run using its in-process gate path. Both can operate on the same worktree, and the old executor's result can outlive the release that created it.
findings.suggestion: Detect the running daemon's release through a record maintained by both old and new releases, and stop executor jobs when that record changes or cannot establish a matching release.
findings.failure_scenario: A new daemon starts an in-place gate, then is rolled back to the base release while the executor remains alive. The old daemon does not update executor.daemonRelease and starts its own gate while the executor continues the existing one.

findings.title: Restart cancels running targeted and timeout retries
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A saved targeted regression retry, baseline retry, or timeout retry is rejected even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease match. The resumed stage cancels that job and starts earlier gate work again, contrary to the requested reattachment coverage for targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the recorded retry at its original call site and attach to its matching live job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts during a long regression-retry-targeted job. On resume, the initial gate path rejects and cancels the saved handle, then reruns the full initial gate instead of receiving the retry result.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor blocks fallback indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined solely by PID and birth time; no heartbeat freshness is recorded. If the executor remains alive but stops processing its event loop, its job lease expires and sweep marks the job failed, but waitStopped continues waiting as long as the process exists. The daemon cannot complete cancellation or fall back, even after the lease and attempt deadline expire.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for a live executor that no longer acknowledges cancellation, without starting another gate until its processes are confirmed stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is suspended or its event loop hangs during a gate. The lease expires, but the daemon remains in waitStopped indefinitely because the executor PID still has the recorded birth time.

The targeted executor test could not start because the checkout is missing the entities package: `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` reported `Cannot find package 'entities'`. The findings below are based on code inspection.

findings.title: Rollback to an older daemon leaves the old executor running
findings.detail: Release-change detection depends entirely on the daemon writing executor.daemonRelease. A release predating this change never writes that setting, so after a rollback it retains the newer release SHA. The executor therefore continues renewing and running its jobs while the older daemon resumes the run using its in-process gate path. Both can operate on the same worktree, and the old executor's result can outlive the release that created it.
findings.suggestion: Detect the running daemon's release through a record maintained by both old and new releases, and stop executor jobs when that record changes or cannot establish a matching release.
findings.failure_scenario: A new daemon starts an in-place gate, then is rolled back to the base release while the executor remains alive. The old daemon does not update executor.daemonRelease and starts its own gate while the executor continues the existing one.

findings.title: Restart cancels running targeted and timeout retries
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A saved targeted regression retry, baseline retry, or timeout retry is rejected even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease match. The resumed stage cancels that job and starts earlier gate work again, contrary to the requested reattachment coverage for targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the recorded retry at its original call site and attach to its matching live job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts during a long regression-retry-targeted job. On resume, the initial gate path rejects and cancels the saved handle, then reruns the full initial gate instead of receiving the retry result.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor blocks fallback indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined solely by PID and birth time; no heartbeat freshness is recorded. If the executor remains alive but stops processing its event loop, its job lease expires and sweep marks the job failed, but waitStopped continues waiting as long as the process exists. The daemon cannot complete cancellation or fall back, even after the lease and attempt deadline expire.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for a live executor that no longer acknowledges cancellation, without starting another gate until its processes are confirmed stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is suspended or its event loop hangs during a gate. The lease expires, but the daemon remains in waitStopped indefinitely because the executor PID still has the recorded birth time.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot be resumed
findings.detail: The resume filter accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during a targeted regression or baseline retry therefore cancels its live in-place job and starts the stage over, despite the requirement to reattach to targeted retries. In the round path, the initial-purpose check encounters the retry handle first and cancels it before retry logic is reached.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough stage progress to resume the recorded retry purpose and its inputs, then attach to that job before restarting earlier gate work.
findings.failure_scenario: A long targeted retry is leased by the executor when the daemon restarts; the resumed engine cancels it and reruns the initial suite and retry.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic with job creation
findings.detail: The scan for existing jobs happens before the handle is saved and the job is inserted, without a reservation or a lease-time worktree check. Two concurrent starts for the same cwd can both observe no job, enqueue separately, and be leased by different executor processes. Their checks then modify the same worktree concurrently.
findings.suggestion: Enforce worktree ownership atomically when reserving or leasing an in-place job, and retain it until process cleanup is confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: Two gate starts for the same worktree pass the empty scan before either attaches; two executor processes lease the resulting rows and run both suites at once.

findings.title: A live process is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; executors never publish a heartbeat. A hung or stopped executor process remains eligible indefinitely. Once its job lease expires, waitStopped also waits indefinitely because it sees that same process as alive, so the daemon cannot finish fallback or make progress on the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Record and check a renewable executor heartbeat, and provide a bounded, safe recovery path for an executor that remains alive but no longer renews its job.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor process stops responding while running a check but remains alive. The lease expires and the job is marked failed, yet the daemon waits forever for stopped to become true.

findings.title: One executor serializes all gates regardless of configured capacity
findings.detail: The polling loop awaits the entire gate before looking for another job. With the normal single executor process, maxConcurrentGates greater than one has no effect on in-place jobs: independent worktrees queue behind the first suite even when slots are free.
findings.suggestion: Run leased jobs concurrently up to the configured capacity while each job independently holds its gate slot and lease.
findings.failure_scenario: With maxConcurrentGates set to two, two runs enqueue independent long suites; the second is not leased until the first finishes.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback repositories
findings.detail: When the configured gate executor is LAN, the in-place flag is ignored. The LAN executor runs repositories outside its allowlist directly in the daemon, so enabling the executor does not protect those local gates from daemon restarts.
findings.suggestion: Use the in-place executor as the local fallback for repositories that are not dispatched to LAN workers.
findings.failure_scenario: With LAN gates configured for one repository and the in-place executor enabled, a gate in another repository runs in the daemon and restarts from scratch after a daemon restart.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A recorded in-place targeted retry is therefore cancelled even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, release, and lease still match. The resumed stage starts the earlier gate flow again instead of receiving the retry result.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching retry and allow its purpose through the resume path.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a `baseline-retry-targeted` or `regression-retry-targeted` job is running. On resume, the job is cancelled and the check runs again.

findings.title: Executor availability is based on process existence rather than a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor rows contain no heartbeat timestamp, and availability only checks whether the recorded PID and birth time still exist. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. Its queued jobs wait for the pickup timeout instead of immediately falling back, and a stalled executor holding a job can leave cancellation waiting indefinitely in `waitStopped`.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and make stop confirmation handle an executor that is alive but no longer responding.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but stops servicing its event loop. The daemon selects it for a new gate, or waits for it to stop a cancelled gate, even though it cannot make progress.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback gates
findings.detail: The opt-in in-place executor is selected only when the configured gate executor is `local`. With LAN configured, repositories outside the LAN allowlist use `lanExecutor`'s in-process local fallback even when the in-place executor is enabled and alive. Those local gates still die on daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local fallback through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure LAN gates for repository A, enable the executor, and run a gate for repository B. The gate runs in the daemon rather than in the executor, so a daemon restart interrupts it.

Reviewed identity selection, configuration validation, GitHub call paths, approval handling, and secret isolation. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout is missing the entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk dependencies.

findings.title: Key validation does not verify that the daemon can read the file
findings.detail: Startup checks the file's owner-read mode bit but neither verifies ownership nor attempts to open it. A regular 0600 file owned by another user passes validation even though the daemon cannot read it. Startup succeeds, then every GitHub operation for an App repository fails when the provider attempts to sign a JWT. The request requires startup to refuse an unreadable key with a clear reason.
findings.suggestion: Verify that the key is readable by the daemon during configuration loading, and reject it with a clear error before startup completes.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure private_key_path to a traversable regular 0600 file owned by another user; loadConfig accepts it, but the first App token exchange fails to read the key.

findings.title: Key validation accepts modes other than the required 0600
findings.detail: The condition accepts any mode with owner-read set and no group or world permission, including 0400 and 0700, despite the requirement and error message specifying mode 0600. A focused evaluation of the condition with `bun -e 'for (const mode of [0o400, 0o600, 0o700]) console.log(mode.toString(8), (mode & 0o077) === 0 && Boolean(mode & 0o400) ? "accepted" : "rejected")'` printed `400 accepted`, `600 accepted`, and `700 accepted`.
findings.suggestion: Compare the permission bits against 0600 and update the test that currently expects 0400 to be accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured key file has mode 0700 or 0400; startup accepts it instead of refusing the configuration.

findings.title: An App key inside a checkout remains readable by agents and gates
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any private key path, but the change does not exclude that path from agent or gate filesystem access. Both can read their checkout, so file mode 0600 does not protect a key there from processes running as the same user. This violates the requirement that the App key never reach an agent or gate.
findings.suggestion: Reject key paths reachable by agents or gates, or enforce a read denial for the resolved key path across every confinement backend.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator sets private_key_path to a 0600 PEM file in a repository checkout. An agent or gate running in that checkout reads the PEM and can sign App JWTs.

findings.title: Startup does not verify that the key is actually readable
findings.detail: The check uses stat and permission bits but never checks whether the daemon can read the file or owns it. A 0600 regular file owned by another user passes validation even though the daemon cannot read it. Startup succeeds, and configured GitHub operations fail later when signing is attempted. The check also accepts mode 0400 despite the requested 0600 requirement.
findings.suggestion: Validate ownership and actual readability at startup, and enforce the requested mode.

findings.title: Protect App keys located outside the config directory
findings.detail: The configuration accepts an absolute private key path, but the read policy only adds the config directory to its protected paths. A key placed elsewhere can therefore be readable by an agent or gate whose permitted filesystem includes that location, contrary to the requirement that the key never reach either.
findings.suggestion: Add the resolved key path to the shared agent and gate read-deny policy, or reject paths outside a directory already protected by that policy.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator configures private_key_path to a 0600 file in a repository checkout; an agent working in that checkout can read the file.

findings.title: Verify key ownership and readability at startup
findings.detail: The mode check treats the file owner's read bit as proof that the daemon can read the file, without checking who owns it or attempting to open it. A 0600 file owned by another user passes configuration validation even when the daemon cannot read it; authentication then fails only when a GitHub operation is attempted.
findings.suggestion: Validate that the file is owned by the daemon user and can be opened for reading during startup, while retaining the restrictive permission checks.
findings.failure_scenario: private_key_path points to another user's 0600 regular file in a searchable directory; startup succeeds and the first configured App operation fails to sign.

findings.title: Validate that the key is owned and readable at startup
findings.detail: The check inspects permission bits but does not verify file ownership or actually open the file. A regular file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes validation even though the daemon cannot read it, so startup succeeds and configured GitHub operations fail later. The check also accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite the requested mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Require the specified mode and owner, and verify that the daemon can open the key during configuration loading; report a clear startup error if any check fails.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key path points to another user's 0600 regular file in a searchable directory. stat succeeds, loadConfig accepts it, and the first App token exchange fails when readFileSync cannot open it.

findings.title: Validate the actual signing key at startup
findings.detail: Startup uses `statSync`, which follows symlinks, and checks neither the file owner nor whether the key can be opened. The signing path later uses `O_NOFOLLOW` and rejects files owned by another user. Consequently, the daemon can start successfully with an App configuration that can never obtain a token; it also accepts modes such as 0400 despite the stated 0600 requirement.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same ownership, regular-file, permission, and openability checks at startup that are used when signing, and enforce the required mode consistently.

findings.title: Validate key ownership and readability at startup
findings.detail: Startup checks the file type and permission bits with stat, but does not verify that the current user owns or can open the file. It also follows symlinks, although the later signing operation rejects them. Consequently, configurations that cannot safely use the key are accepted at startup and fail only when an App repository first makes a GitHub call. The check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite requiring mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Use the same no-follow open and descriptor-based owner, mode, and readability validation at startup as the signing path, and enforce the required mode consistently.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured key is a symlink to a mode-0600 regular file, or is owned by another user with mode 0600. Configuration loads and the daemon starts, but the first App token exchange fails when signingKey rejects or cannot open the file.

findings.title: Authentication rejections in retry events are lost when the session times out
findings.detail: The captured stream contains structured 401 authentication failures in system api_retry events, but the parser ignores them. If the invocation deadline or watchdog ends the CLI before it emits its final assistant/result events, runClaude returns timeout or stuck without failureClass. On a worker that result is returned instead of falling back locally; on the coordinator it is treated as a task-level result, so an implement round can proceed to gates and consume the round budget despite never authenticating.
findings.suggestion: Track structured authentication retry events and preserve that classification when the process ends without a later successful session, while retaining explicit caller cancellation semantics.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude emits an api_retry event with error_status 401 and error authentication_failed, then the invocation times out before the final result event.

findings.title: Older workers still report authentication failures as completed rounds
findings.detail: The coordinator recognizes a worker authentication failure only through the new optional failureClass field. A worker running the previous release neither classifies the Claude response nor sends that field, so its authentication failure remains an ordinary error and is returned as the round result. Updating the coordinator while LAN workers are still on the previous release therefore leaves the reported failure mode active.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-compatible worker reporting or dispatch strategy that prevents an older worker's unclassified authentication rejection from being accepted as a completed round.
findings.failure_scenario: A newly deployed coordinator dispatches an implement job to an older LAN worker whose Claude token is expired; the worker reports status error without failureClass, and the coordinator continues to gates.

findings.title: Treating every terminal 401 as a session that never ran can repeat work
findings.detail: The classifier does not distinguish a login rejection before the first model call from an authentication failure after successful turns. If a token expires during an editing session, the agent may already have edited files or performed tool side effects. The new classification makes Context.invoke invoke another candidate on the same worktree; on a worker, its changes are published and adopted before the local fallback runs. That can repeat side effects or make the fallback operate on a partial implementation while treating the first session as though it could not run.
findings.suggestion: Track whether the session completed any successful model turns or tool calls, and use the no-session authentication fallback only when the structured stream establishes that no work ran. Handle a later authentication failure as an interrupted session with its existing work preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude successfully edits a file, then its OAuth token expires on a later API request and the result reports api_error_status 401. The coordinator invokes a second implementer against the partially edited checkout, or adopts the worker commit and runs the round locally again.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos and is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The request requires lifecycle updates for every start path, including CLI and MCP runs, regardless of whether that repository participates in automatic issue selection.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked GitHub issues independently of the trusted queue list.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` targets a GitHub repository with no issue queue configured. No lifecycle label or comment is ever written.

findings.title: Status transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are discovered only from the current status, and a pending checkpoint is created only when reconciliation reaches that comment. findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it between two queue polls. The next poll sees resolved and never posts the needs-you reason.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be picked again
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed. findings.suggestion: Make the existing admission check account for the latest locally linked run and its failure while lifecycle writes are pending, including runs linked through Closes directives.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #42 fails. Deleting its in-progress label succeeds, adding failed returns an error, and the same poll admits issue 42 using its old priority label.

findings.title: A newer run can be overwritten by an older reconciliation
findings.detail: The latest-run map is captured once before any GitHub awaits. If another run for the issue is created during a label request, the old run remains authorized by this stale map and can write its terminal label over the new run's in-progress state. Re-reading only the old run does not detect the newer claimant.
findings.suggestion: Recheck which run is latest after awaited GitHub calls and before each label mutation and checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of a failed run waits for the issue's labels, an owner starts a new run for the same issue. The old reconciliation resumes and writes limitless:failed despite the newer active run.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation runs only when the issue queue is configured with trusted accounts, and it skips repositories outside that queue. The requested lifecycle applies to all start paths, including manual, MCP, label, and comment triggers; those paths can operate for repositories that are not configured for automatic queue pickup.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for every linked issue in a configured repository.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts a run with `Closes #7` in a repository with no `[github.queue]` configuration. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The reconciler creates terminal and needs-human events solely from the current run status. It records a pending comment only after observing that status, so a transition that occurs and is resolved between polls is permanently lost. The same applies across a daemon restart before the first poll observes the transition.
findings.suggestion: Durably record lifecycle events and their publication text when the corresponding run transitions occur, then reconcile those records on each poll.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and the owner resumes it before the next poll. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever posted.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority-label event, even when that label is no longer applied. A different priority label that was applied before the failure can remain current and supply `approved`, so the two checks together admit an issue without a current priority label that was applied after the failure.
findings.suggestion: Require the qualifying post-failure event to be the latest application of a currently applied, trusted priority label.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. After failure, a trusted user briefly applies and removes `priority:9`; the queue admits the issue using the old `priority:2` and the removed label's event.

findings.title: A failed label transition can expose an issue to another pickup
findings.detail: The transition removes `limitless:in-progress` before adding `limitless:failed`, then continues queue admission even if the add fails. The existing latest-run lookup covers issue-source runs, but not manual runs linked through `Closes #n`. Consequently a failed manual run can leave the issue with neither status label and no applicable latest-run guard.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed while a failed lifecycle transition is pending, including for prompt-linked runs, or ensure the failure label is applied before releasing the in-progress label.
findings.failure_scenario: A manual run linked by `Closes #7` fails. Deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails; the same poll can pick the still-priority-labelled issue without a new approval.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs through the issue queue and filters every linked issue through `lifecycleManaged`, which requires the repository to be in `githubQueue.repos` and a trusted account to be configured. The requested lifecycle applies to every start path, including manual and MCP runs, independently of whether issue pickup is enabled for that repository.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from all supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A manual `limitless run` with `Closes #123` targets a repository that is not in the issue queue configuration. The run receives no issue labels or lifecycle comments.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments contain only a generic status and UI link; neither includes the run's reason. This leaves issue watchers unable to see why the run failed or needs their help, even when the reason is safe to publish.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using the fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` with a specific question in `run.error`; the issue comment says only `needs you: see ...` and never conveys the question.

findings.title: Blocked publication permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done and no fallback is posted. The same happens if a pending body fails the check on retry. The request explicitly requires a fixed safe message when text is blocked.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a fixed, checked fallback body instead of marking the effect complete without a write.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the UI URL or run text, causing `checkPublicationText` to throw. The lifecycle comment is permanently suppressed, including after restart.

findings.title: Transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The reconciler derives comment events only from the current run snapshot. If a run enters `needs_human` and is resolved or resumed before the next poll, that event is never persisted and its comment is lost. A restart before the next poll has the same effect. Polling the current status cannot provide the requested durable checkpoint for each lifecycle event.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the run transitions, then have the poller deliver those recorded effects.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters `needs_human`, and an owner resolves it before the next queue poll. Reconciliation sees only `resolved` and never posts the needs-you comment.

findings.title: A failed run can be readmitted before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the latest run failed but the failure label is absent, admission falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after `finishedAt`. Lifecycle label writes can fail or be delayed, and reconciliation removes in-progress before adding failed, so a priority application in that interval can satisfy admission even though it preceded the failure label. This violates the required ordering and can start a new run before anyone sees the failure label.
findings.suggestion: For a locally recorded failed run, require evidence of its failure label followed by a trusted priority application, including while the label write is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the owner reapplies a priority label, and the failed-label write is delayed or fails. The next poll sees no failed label and accepts the priority event as re-approval.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs for repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in another configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, despite the requirement covering every start path. If the queue is disabled entirely, the reconciler is not started at all.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked issues independently of queue admission configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` targets a configured repository absent from githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or lifecycle comment is posted.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both messages always contain only a generic UI link and never use the run's error or reason. The requested fallback is intended for text blocked by the publication check, but this implementation uses the fallback even for ordinary safe reasons. The added tests explicitly assert that the reason is absent.
findings.suggestion: Include the sanitized, redacted reason when publication permits it, and use a fixed fallback only when it does not.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with the safe error `typecheck failed`; the issue comment says only `failed: see ...`, leaving issue watchers without the requested reason.

findings.title: A blocked comment is permanently discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: When publication validation rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting anything. The same happens if a pending body fails validation on retry. This loses the required lifecycle notification rather than posting the specified fixed message.
findings.suggestion: Prepare and checkpoint a safe fixed fallback comment when validation blocks the original text, and retry its delivery normally.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL contains a private string, so checkPublicationText rejects the start comment; the effect is marked done and no start comment is ever posted.

findings.title: State transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The reconciler derives events only from the current run snapshot. A needs-human or failed state that changes before the next poll leaves no durable effect, so its comment and label change are lost. Polling also cannot reconstruct an intermediate transition after a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when run state changes, then let the poller deliver the recorded effects.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resolved by the owner before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or comment.

findings.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is written
findings.detail: If the failure-label write fails, eligibility falls back to accepting a priority event after finishedAt even though that event occurred before the failure label was applied. For CLI runs linked by `Closes #n`, latestIssueRun does not find the run at all, so even the existing priority label can admit the issue. Reconciliation catches the write failure and continues to queue selection in the same poll.
findings.suggestion: Use durable failure state for all linked run paths in the existing admission check, and require a trusted priority application after the failure-label event.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for an approved issue fails, the GitHub label write returns an error, and the same poll sees the old priority label and creates another run.

findings.detail: The only caller of lifecycle reconciliation is the issue queue, which does not start without configured queue repositories and trusted accounts. Reconciliation also filters linked issues through the queue repository list. findings.detail: Comments are created from the run's current status only, and each status has a single effect key for the entire run. A needs-human episode that resolves before the next poll is never recorded; a later needs-human episode is also suppressed if an earlier one was recorded. Neither transition has a durable event checkpoint.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events when transitions occur, with a durable identifier for each episode, and let polling deliver those records.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll. The issue never receives the needs-you comment or label for that transition.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both messages are fixed strings and never include the run's error or other reason. Owners therefore cannot see why the run failed or needs their attention, even when the reason is safe to publish.

findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link or run identifier; the started or terminal comment is marked done and never appears on the issue.

findings.detail: When the latest run failed but the failed label is absent, eligibility falls back to accepting a trusted priority event after `finishedAt`. A failed lifecycle label write does not prevent queue admission, so that approval can precede the eventual failure-label application, contrary to the required ordering.
findings.suggestion: Require evidence of the failure label and a later trusted priority application for a failed latest run, including while the label write is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: The failed-label API call fails, a trusted user reapplies priority after the run finishes, and the next poll admits the issue before `limitless:failed` has ever been applied.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue is enabled, and it filters out repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`. The request requires updates for linked issues from every start path; it does not require the repository to opt into automatic queue admission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run links an issue in a repository that is not in `githubQueue.repos`. It receives no lifecycle label or comment.

findings.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is written
findings.detail: When the failure label write fails, the issue has no `limitless:failed` label, so eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after `finishedAt`. Reconciliation logs the write failure and proceeds to queue admission in the same poll. That permits approval before the required failure-label event.
findings.suggestion: Keep the issue ineligible while its failure label is pending, and require the trusted priority event to follow the recorded failure-label application.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the owner reapplies a priority label, and GitHub rejects the pending failure-label write. The following queue query sees the post-finish priority event and starts another run even though no priority event followed a failure label.

findings.title: Polling current status loses lifecycle transitions
findings.detail: The reconciler creates needs-human, failure, and cancellation effects only from the run's current status. Those effects are not recorded when the transition occurs, so a transition that begins and ends between polls is invisible. The single effect key per status also prevents a later needs-human episode from producing its own comment.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it happens and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever recorded or delivered; a second needs-human episode is also suppressed if the first was observed.

findings.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments contain only a UI link. The requested lifecycle updates require the reason, subject to credential redaction and the private-strings check.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after sanitizing and checking it, with a fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe, useful error message; the issue receives only `failed: see …`, leaving watchers without the required reason.

findings.title: A blocked comment is discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: If the private-strings check rejects a comment, the catch marks the effect done and posts nothing. The same happens if the check rejects the saved body during delivery. This permanently loses the required notification rather than posting the specified fixed safe message.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a fixed, checked fallback body when the original comment cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL contains a private string. The start comment fails publication checking, is marked done, and is never posted or retried.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the configured issue queue
findings.detail: The only caller of lifecycle reconciliation is the issue queue, which does not start without configured queue repositories and trusted accounts. Reconciliation also filters linked issues through the queue repository list. Consequently, CLI, MCP, and trigger runs for other repositories receive no lifecycle labels or comments, despite the requirement covering every start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover linked issues in repositories where runs can be started.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in `githubQueue.repos`; no lifecycle update is sent.

findings.title: Polling loses transitions that occur between observations
findings.detail: Comments are created from the run's current status only, and each status has a single effect key for the entire run. A needs-human episode that resolves before the next poll is never recorded; a later needs-human episode is also suppressed if an earlier one was recorded. Neither transition has a durable event checkpoint.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events when transitions occur, with a durable identifier for each episode, and let polling deliver those records.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll. The issue never receives the needs-you comment or label for that transition.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both messages are fixed strings and never include the run's error or other reason. Owners therefore cannot see why the run failed or needs their attention, even when the reason is safe to publish.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using a fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a public error such as `tests failed`; the issue comment says only `failed: see ...` and omits that reason.

findings.title: Blocked publication permanently drops the required comment

findings.suggestion: Create and deliver a fixed fallback comment when the original text fails the publication check.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link or run identifier; the started or terminal comment is marked done and never appears on the issue.

structured.summary: The lifecycle implementation misses several required paths and can admit a failed issue before its failure label is applied. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue is enabled, and it filters out repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`. The request requires updates for linked issues from every start path; it does not require the repository to opt into automatic queue admission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run links an issue in a repository that is not in `githubQueue.repos`. It receives no lifecycle label or comment.

findings.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is written
findings.detail: When the failure label write fails, the issue has no `limitless:failed` label, so eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after `finishedAt`. Reconciliation logs the write failure and proceeds to queue admission in the same poll. That permits approval before the required failure-label event.
findings.suggestion: Keep the issue ineligible while its failure label is pending, and require the trusted priority event to follow the recorded failure-label application.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the owner reapplies a priority label, and GitHub rejects the pending failure-label write. The following queue query sees the post-finish priority event and starts another run even though no priority event followed a failure label.

findings.title: Polling current status loses lifecycle transitions
findings.detail: The reconciler creates needs-human, failure, and cancellation effects only from the run's current status. Those effects are not recorded when the transition occurs, so a transition that begins and ends between polls is invisible. The single effect key per status also prevents a later needs-human episode from producing its own comment.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it happens and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever recorded or delivered; a second needs-human episode is also suppressed if the first was observed.

findings.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments contain only a UI link. The requested lifecycle updates require the reason, subject to credential redaction and the private-strings check.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after sanitizing and checking it, with a fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe, useful error message; the issue receives only `failed: see …`, leaving watchers without the required reason.

findings.title: A blocked comment is discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: If the private-strings check rejects a comment, the catch marks the effect done and posts nothing. The same happens if the check rejects the saved body during delivery. This permanently loses the required notification rather than posting the specified fixed safe message.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a fixed, checked fallback body when the original comment cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL contains a private string. The start comment fails publication checking, is marked done, and is never posted or retried.

findings.title: In-flight older workers can publish an ungranted workflow
findings.detail: The publication guard runs only in the worker's newly deployed code. A worker that leased an edit job before the coordinator upgrade can continue executing its older code after the coordinator restarts, and its existing lease remains valid. That worker can commit and push a workflow before the upgraded coordinator audits or inspects the result. Release parity prevents new leases to an older worker but does not cancel an already leased job.
findings.suggestion: Invalidate or safely drain pre-upgrade publication-capable agent leases before the new policy takes effect, or enforce the workflow check at a publication boundary controlled by the upgraded coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: An older worker has an active edit job when the daemon is upgraded. Its agent adds .github/workflows/ci.yml without an allowance; the old worker pushes the commit directly, triggering the workflow before the new coordinator can block delivery.

Traced rejection persistence, rollback, and scheduler recovery. The targeted restart test could not run because the checkout is missing the 'entities' package; Bun reported an import error before executing any tests.

findings.title: Keep an interrupted rejection eligible for scheduler recovery
findings.detail: The rejection checkpoint also sets the run to `needs_human` before rollback starts. On daemon startup, the scheduler recovers only `running` and `waiting_input` runs, so it never invokes `rollbackRejectedMerge` for this checkpoint. The new restart tests call `executeRun` directly, bypassing that scheduler behavior. A rollback error or shutdown is likewise caught and returned as `needs_human` without arranging another attempt.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while keeping the run recoverable, then set the terminal status after rollback completes. Exercise the restart through the scheduler rather than invoking the engine directly.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon stops immediately after the rejection checkpoint or after `reset` but before `clean` and the state save. After restart, the run remains `needs_human` with the checkout and persisted rollback fields only partially restored; rollback never finishes.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents interrupted rollback from resuming
findings.detail: The rejection is saved with status needs_human before rollback starts. On daemon restart, the scheduler only requeues interrupted running and waiting_input runs, so it never invokes rollbackRejectedMerge for this terminal run. The restart tests call executeRun directly even when the stored status is needs_human, bypassing the scheduler behavior they need to verify.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while the run remains recoverable, finish rollback, and only then write the terminal status. Exercise the restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon stops immediately after the rejection checkpoint or after git reset but before the state save. After restart, the run remains needs_human and the checkout or persisted head and gate state remains partially rolled back.

findings.title: An empty repository loses its first command
findings.detail: A successful first poll with no open issues leaves the boundary unset. The next poll then treats all comments present at that time as pre-existing and establishes the boundary from them, even if they were created after the queue was enabled. The new test explicitly expects this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue while the repository has no open issues, then create an issue and post `/limitless fix it` before the next poll. That poll stores the comment timestamp as the boundary, so the command never runs.

findings.title: The initial boundary can precede commands written before enablement
findings.detail: The newest timestamp among currently open issues is not necessarily close to the time the queue was enabled. Comments on closed issues are absent from the response, so a later reopened issue can expose a pre-enablement command whose timestamp is newer than the stored boundary. The poller then runs it.
findings.suggestion: Obtain a GitHub-time enable boundary that also excludes commands on issues that were closed during the first poll.
findings.failure_scenario: The newest open issue was updated January 1; a trusted user commented on a closed issue January 2; the queue is enabled January 3; that issue is reopened January 4. Its January 2 command is newer than the stored January 1 boundary and starts a run.

findings.title: A marker anywhere in a legitimate request silently suppresses it
findings.detail: The factory-comment check rejects any command whose body contains `<!-- limitless-`, regardless of its author or context. A trusted user's valid request can include that text as data, and the command is skipped on every poll without a refusal record.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments using their author or a narrowly validated factory marker, rather than searching the entire request for a substring.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless investigate why <!-- limitless-lifecycle:... --> appears in this issue`. The command meets the requested syntax but never starts a run.

findings.title: Identity failures bypass the factory-author exclusion
findings.detail: When App identity lookup fails, the error is converted to null and slash commands continue to be processed. The author comparison then cannot recognize the factory bot. If that bot is in the trusted list, its command is accepted and recorded despite the requirement that factory-posted comments never run.
findings.suggestion: Leave commands retryable until the factory identity can be established for an App-backed repository.
findings.failure_scenario: The trusted list includes the App bot, its identity lookup temporarily fails, and one of its comments begins `/limitless `. The poll creates a run for the factory's own comment.

findings.title: An initially empty repository loses its first command
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues leaves the boundary unset. When an issue and command subsequently appear, that later poll initializes the boundary from their timestamps and skips the command forever. The first successful poll was supposed to establish the enable boundary, so commands created after it remain actionable.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary even when the first response contains no open issues, and test an empty initial poll followed by a new issue and command.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue for a repository with no open issues, complete a poll, then open an issue and post `/limitless fix it` before the next poll. No run is created on that or later polls.

findings.title: The boundary can precede old commands on closed issues
findings.detail: The initial query includes only open issues, and its newest timestamp can be much older than the actual enable time. A closed issue can already contain a command newer than that timestamp; when reopened after enablement, the old command passes the boundary check and starts a run. The existing reopened-issue test covers only a command older than the stored timestamp.
findings.suggestion: Derive an enable boundary that also excludes commands already present on issues closed during the first poll, and cover this ordering in a test.
findings.failure_scenario: The only open issue was last updated Monday; a closed issue received a command Tuesday; the queue is enabled Wednesday; the closed issue is reopened Thursday. Its Tuesday command is processed because it is newer than Monday's stored boundary.

findings.title: Identity lookup failure bypasses the factory-author exclusion
findings.detail: An identity lookup error is converted to null, but slash commands continue processing. With no bot login, the factory-author comparison cannot match, so a trusted factory bot's own slash command can create a run. This violates the requirement that factory-posted comments never start runs and consumes the comment before identity lookup can recover.
findings.suggestion: Leave slash commands unprocessed when the posting identity cannot be established, or otherwise identify factory authors without failing open.
findings.failure_scenario: The App bot login is in the trusted list, its comment begins `/limitless `, and `githubIdentity` temporarily fails. The next poll creates a run from the bot's comment.

findings.title: A marker anywhere in a valid request silently suppresses it
findings.detail: The command filter rejects any body containing `<!-- limitless-`, regardless of its author or context. A trusted user's otherwise valid request can legitimately quote or ask to change a factory marker, but it will be skipped on every poll and never recorded or executed.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments using the posting identity or a precise provenance check rather than rejecting arbitrary request text.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless Fix the <!-- limitless-status --> marker` after enablement. The command is never run.

findings.title: Replay timestamps evidence at recovery rather than execution
findings.detail: A durable LAN or in-place result can remain stored for an arbitrary time before the daemon resumes. The observation uses Date.now() during replay, so its observed_at no longer reflects when the failure occurred. Promotion uses that timestamp as its seven-day evidence window, which can both correlate failures that actually occurred too far apart and miss failures that occurred close together.
findings.suggestion: Persist the execution completion time with the durable result and use it when recording or replaying its observations.

findings.title: Redaction can collapse distinct checks into one observation key
findings.detail: The unique key uses the redacted name. If two distinct check names redact to the same string, the second insert is silently discarded by ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING even though both checks executed and failed. The requirement calls for one observation per failed check.
findings.suggestion: Preserve a collision-resistant execution identity for the key while keeping the stored display name redacted.
findings.failure_scenario: Two checks have names containing different registered credentials that both redact to the same placeholder, and both fail in the same execution. Only one failure observation is stored.

findings.title: Replay completed in-place results across a daemon upgrade
findings.detail: Resume still requires the in-place executor's canResume check, which requires the stored request's releaseSha, environment and daemon port to match the current daemon even when the job is already done. If any differs, resume cancels the handle and starts a new execution without recording the completed result. This loses a failure when a deployment restarts the daemon between result completion and the evidence checkpoint.
findings.suggestion: Permit replay of an already completed in-place result independently of the compatibility checks needed to continue a live job, and cover an upgrade between completion and the evidence checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: An in-place job finishes with a failing check, the daemon stops before the evidence insert, and a new release starts with a different build SHA. canResume returns false, the completed job is discarded, and a passing replacement execution leaves no observation for the original failure.

findings.title: Replay timestamps failures at recovery rather than execution
findings.detail: A retained LAN or in-place result that was not recorded before a crash receives Date.now() when it is replayed. A long interruption therefore changes the evidence timestamp and can either create or suppress an undeclared-requirement promotion, whose seven-day window is defined by when the executions were observed.
findings.suggestion: Persist the execution's observation time with the durable result and reuse it when replaying that result.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker failure completes, the daemon crashes before the evidence checkpoint, and the run resumes eight days later. A matching failure at another location shortly after the original execution is no longer within seven days of the replayed row.

findings.title: A replayed timeout is recorded as a retry instead of a stage rerun
findings.detail: The earlier-stage shortcut runs before checking firstAttempt. If a retained result was already recorded before shutdown, replay occurs under a new stage row; a subsequent successful timeout rerun is therefore recorded as retry_passed instead of rerun_passed. The class remains load, but the durable history misstates what happened. A targeted probe produced the wrong result: `bun -e 'import { observationHistory } from "./src/gates/failure-class.ts"; const c = {name:"test", verdict:"pass", blocking:false, result:{name:"test",command:"test",ok:true,exitCode:0,durationMs:1,output:"",firstAttempt:{name:"test",command:"test",ok:false,exitCode:null,durationMs:1,output:"",timedOut:true}}}; console.log(observationHistory(c,true));'` printed `retry_passed`.
findings.suggestion: Identify a replay of the same execution separately from a new primary execution, and preserve the timeout rerun history for the replayed observation.
findings.failure_scenario: An in-place timeout is recorded, shutdown retains its handle, and the resumed stage reattaches to that result before its timeout rerun passes.

Reviewed the service lifecycle, recovery paths, executor release handling, and tests. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout has incomplete or incompatible dependencies: zod lacks prefault and entities is missing.

Reviewed the deploy, installation, recovery, and executor release-following paths. The focused test command could not run because the checkout's installed dependencies are inconsistent: zod lacks prefault and entities is missing.

findings.title: Stop the executor when daemon replacement fails during installation
findings.detail: The installation loop replaces and health-checks the daemon before it reaches the executor. If daemon replacement or its health check fails, the error path restores the daemon and exits without shutting down the existing executor. This violates the requirement that a failed install leave no executor running on an unconfirmed release, particularly after a packaged upgrade has changed the executable behind the stable path.
findings.suggestion: Ensure a failed installation confirms the installed executor is unloaded and disabled, including failures that occur before the executor's own replacement begins, and cover the daemon-replacement failure path.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is loaded, a packaged upgrade changes the stable executable, and service install fails while starting or health-checking the replacement daemon. Installation exits with the existing executor still loaded and enabled.

findings.title: A loaded executor that never served the old release can remain stale after deploy
findings.detail: Reconciliation treats any loaded executor as sufficient and does not establish which release it is running. An executor only exits on a release mismatch after it has observed its own release as the daemon release. If a deploy moves the daemon before that first observation, the old executor stays loaded and idles indefinitely, while the deploy reports success.
findings.suggestion: Ensure successful deploy reconciliation establishes that the loaded executor will run the target release even if it never observed the previous daemon release.
findings.failure_scenario: A successful install starts executor A, then a deploy to B restarts the daemon before the executor's first poll observes A. The executor sees B while still unserved and keeps idling; reconciliation sees its unit loaded and returns successfully.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise a running in-place job
findings.detail: The added restart test checks fake launchctl calls and an intent file, but it does not start an in-place job or verify that the restarted daemon reattaches and that the command runs exactly once. Those are explicit acceptance criteria and are not established by the call-log assertion.
findings.suggestion: Extend the existing real-process restart coverage with a running in-place job, then assert reattachment and one command execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that leaves the executor untouched but causes the restarted daemon to duplicate or lose its in-place job would pass the added restart assertions.

Reviewed executor installation, deploy recovery, rollback, and release-following paths. Targeted tests could not run because the available dependencies lack Zod's prefault method and the entities package.

Reviewed executor control, installation recovery, deploy rollback, release following, and restart behavior. Targeted tests could not start because installed dependencies are incomplete or incompatible: Zod lacks prefault and the entities package is missing.

findings.title: Failed executor inspection leaves the replacement enabled
findings.detail: Reconciliation enables the replacement label before inspecting whether it is loaded. If that inspection times out or otherwise returns an unknown state, this early throw skips executor restoration and shutdown. The replacement plist and enabled label remain in place, so launchd can load it at the next login even though installation failed. The existing inspection-reconcile test explicitly expects this retained replacement and enable call.
findings.suggestion: On executor inspection failures, retain the journal and attempt the fail-closed shutdown and restoration path using the non-interrupted command runner; report recovery instructions if shutdown cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: During executor replacement, launchctl enable succeeds but launchctl print times out. Installation exits with an error while the new plist remains enabled; a subsequent login loads it without a successful reconciliation.

findings.title: Treat a timed-out disable as unconfirmed
findings.detail: shutdownExecutor accepts a launchctl disable result whenever exitCode is zero, even if timedOut is true. The subprocess wrapper explicitly permits this combination when a process exits successfully after its deadline. The helper can therefore report a confirmed shutdown and allow rollback to change the checkout without confirmation that the executor is disabled. The enable and bootstrap checks have the same omission, so reconciliation can also report success after a timed-out command.
findings.suggestion: Reject timedOut results as well as nonzero exit codes for executor launchctl operations, and cover the exit-zero timeout case for disable and reconciliation.
findings.failure_scenario: During rollback, launchctl disable exceeds its deadline and exits zero after termination without confirming the disabled state. shutdownExecutor returns successfully, and rollback checks out the previous release while the executor may still be enabled for a later login.
