findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
findings.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
findings.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 introduces `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha);`; the base release's startup lacks this write. src/gates/inplace.ts:39 detects changes solely with `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`, and lines 53–57 otherwise renew the lease. src/db/workers.ts:388 likewise gates leasing on that persistent setting.
verification.trigger: An executor running a gate survives rollback to the base daemon, with no LAN activity sweeping its job. The base daemon leaves executor.daemonRelease naming the newer release, so the executor continues the gate and can lease remaining matching queued jobs despite the daemon release changing.

findings.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359: `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. Lease expiry marks the job failed at :671–672, but waitStopped at :366–384 loops while `stopped === 0`, attempting recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits this loop before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive but stops making progress during a leased gate. The lease expires, but its process identity still matches, so waitStopped keeps sleeping and fallback cannot start until the executor resumes or exits.

findings.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
findings.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1566 starts purpose "timeout"; :1595 uses "regression-retry-targeted" for targeted retries. On resume, :1536 first requests "initial". src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose` and `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; :35–43 cancels a rejected handle and clears it.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts during a leased targeted or timeout retry. Resuming the gates stage rejects and cancels the saved retry job, then starts gate work again instead of reattaching.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
findings.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

verification.evidence: src/app.ts:186 passes cfg.executorEnabled to gateExecutorFor. However, src/gates/executor.ts:79–81 handles LAN configuration with `return lanExecutor(workers, repos);`, omitting the in-place flag. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults that flag to false, and src/gates/lan.ts:71 directly falls back with `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`. Repository B's gates run in the daemon instead of creating an in-place job, so a daemon restart loses the running execution and requires rerunning it.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error with `catch (error) { workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error))); }`. src/db/workers.ts:626–632 converts an in-place failure to `state='failed'`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles every failed job by starting `local.start(request, controller.signal)` without checking for ConfinementError; lines 147–150 complete and return the fallback result.
verification.trigger: Executor confinement preflight throws ConfinementError; cleanup succeeds and the daemon’s local preflight and checks succeed. The gate returns a passing fallback result instead of preserving the confinement failure.

findings.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
findings.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
findings.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:75–80 sets `stopped=1` only when both process-discovery and cleanup records are empty, then returns to the leasing loop at :29–30. src/db/workers.ts:370 runs recovery only under `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise :384 only sleeps.
verification.trigger: Cancellation finishes with a retained cleanup record after cleanup fails. The executor stays alive and polls other jobs, leaving stopped=0 permanently. The daemon waits indefinitely for confirmation instead of recovering or reporting the unresolved cleanup.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic across concurrent starts
findings.detail: The query for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations. Two daemon-side starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue independently. With two executor processes, each can lease one job and run both gates in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Enforce worktree exclusivity atomically in the database when creating or leasing an in-place job.

AND state='queued'`, without checking for another leased job in the same cwd.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both observe no existing job before either attaches. Both then enqueue distinct jobs. With two live executors and available gate slots, each executor can lease a different job and run checks simultaneously in that worktree.

findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

verification.trigger: An idle executor remains alive but becomes unresponsive. The daemon treats it as available and enqueues a gate rather than immediately using the required no-fresh-heartbeat fallback; execution is delayed until pickup timeout.

findings.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
findings.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. The executor loads configured provider credentials, but it does not receive credentials registered dynamically by the daemon, such as GitHub installation tokens and worker tokens. It redacts and persists check events and results using its own incomplete registry before the daemon sees them, so the daemon’s later redaction cannot remove the copies already stored in gate_jobs.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the executor has the daemon’s complete current redaction set before processing output, or defer persistence of output to a boundary that has that set while preserving restart-safe event handling.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon registers a GitHub installation token during operation, and a gate prints that token. An in-place executor that never registered the token stores it unredacted in the job’s events or result.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1218 keeps registrations in process-local sets: `const credentialValues = new Set<string>()`. src/gates/inplace.ts:65 writes results through `workers.event(...)`, and line 69 calls `workers.complete(...)`. src/db/workers.ts:612–613 stores `this.sanitize(event)`; line 717 stores `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))`. That sanitizer uses process-local redaction (lines 129–133); src/util/private-output.ts:11 builds protection from `registeredCredentials()`, with no synchronization from the daemon.
verification.trigger: A token registered dynamically only in the daemon, absent from the executor’s registrations and private-string policy, appears in gate output. The executor persists the token unredacted in gate_jobs events and result before daemon-side sanitization can protect it.

findings.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
findings.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. The policy uses environment variables such as AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, GH_CONFIG_DIR, and CARGO_HOME to deny credential paths. When those variables differ between the daemon and executor, a credential path known to the daemon can be omitted from the executor’s deny list, weakening the confinement applied to untrusted gate commands.
findings.suggestion: Build the gate’s confinement policy from the same trusted environment used by the daemon, including its credential-path variables, and refuse execution if that policy cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing to a credential file under an otherwise allowed toolchain path, while the executor lacks that variable. A gate can read the file through the in-place executor even though the daemon’s local confinement would deny it.

verification.evidence: src/cli/main.ts:426 starts the executor with `runInplaceExecutor(loadConfig(), sha, controller.signal)`. src/config.ts:455 constructs `readPolicy: configureReadPolicy(raw.sandbox, configDir)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:44–62 captures policy environment from `process.env`, including AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE. src/gates/inplace.ts:27 uses `readPolicyScope.run(cfg.readPolicy, ...)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:144 reads that policy environment, and line 169 includes `env.AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE` among denied credentials; the request’s env never replaces this policy.
verification.trigger: Only the daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE naming a credential file under a readable toolchain path. The executor’s independently constructed policy omits that credential path, allowing its gate to read the file where the daemon’s policy would deny or reject the overlapping allowance.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The request says the local executor covers “the targeted retry” and that a resumed stage with the same stage, round, purpose and SHA attaches to its job. The purpose whitelist excludes both regression retry purposes and baseline retry purposes. On resume, the surrounding stage first asks to resume its initial gate, so it cancels the still-running retry and starts the stage's gate work again.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the recorded retry at its original point, and include its purpose in the resume validation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage treats the handle as a mismatch, cancels the retry and reruns gate work instead of receiving that job's result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)`, whereas :1595 assigns targeted jobs purpose "regression-retry-targeted". src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 rejects that purpose; :35–43 cancels the old execution and clears its persisted handle.

findings.title: Executor liveness is process existence, not a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: The request requires fallback when no executor has a fresh heartbeat and requires the sweep to apply freshness timers against that heartbeat. Executor rows contain no heartbeat timestamp; this method only checks whether the PID and birth time still exist. candidates.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor freshness is determined solely by whether its PID and birth time still match; there is no heartbeat. If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 checks only `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. src/db/workers.ts:365–384 loops while `stopped === 0`, attempts recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`, and otherwise sleeps. src/gates/lan.ts:130–131 awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor stalls while owning a gate, remains alive, and stops renewing. After lease expiry, the daemon marks the job failed but waits indefinitely for stop acknowledgement, blocking fallback and the worktree.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from `executeGate`, including `ConfinementError`, and marks the job failed. The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor cannot verify its Seatbelt confinement, but the daemon's subsequent local confinement check succeeds; the local retry passes and the original security failure is lost.

verification.evidence: src/harness/sandbox.ts:199–200 throws `new ConfinementError("Write confinement not verified: ...")`. src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error and calls `workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error)))`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles every failed in-place job by waiting for it to stop and calling `local.start(request, controller.signal)`. Lines 147–150 return the fallback result without preserving a confinement verdict.
verification.trigger: The executor's confinement verification throws, then the daemon's local verification succeeds. The failed security check becomes an infrastructure fallback and the passing local GateRun replaces it; only a failure diagnostic remains.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and previously leased jobs eventually enter `waitStopped`, which continues waiting as long as that process exists. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.
findings.suggestion: Track executor freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for an unresponsive owner while confirming its gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor hangs while running a gate and stops renewing its lease. The sweep marks the job failed, but `waitStopped` waits indefinitely because the executor PID still exists, so the run never falls back or finishes.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 calls `this.fail(j.id, "Lease expired")`, but src/db/workers.ts:370 permits recovery only if `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`. Executor availability checks only process identity at src/db/workers.ts:359. src/gates/lan.ts:131 waits for stopped before fallback.
verification.trigger: A live executor stops servicing its running job. Its lease expires, but its unchanged PID and birth identity keep waitStopped polling indefinitely; fallback never starts.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The resume whitelist excludes targeted and other retry purposes. When a daemon restarts during a targeted retry, the resumed stage rejects the recorded handle and cancels the surviving job instead of attaching to it. This leaves the requested restart protection incomplete for a gate purpose explicitly named in the request.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the matching retry job and attach to it after restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A long `regression-retry-targeted` job is running when the daemon restarts; the resumed gate stage cancels that job and reruns earlier gate work rather than receiving its result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 uses purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"` for targeted retries. Restart replay enters src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 with purpose `"initial"`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29-30 requires equal purposes and restricts resumable purposes to `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]`; lines 35-43 cancel and clear the rejected job. Initial gates run at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1547.
verification.trigger: A daemon restart interrupts attachment to a running targeted regression retry. The resumed stage rejects its saved handle and cancels the job instead of receiving its result.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: Resume is restricted to baseline, initial and rebase purposes. Targeted retries use baseline-retry-targeted or regression-retry-targeted, so a restart rejects their matching durable handle, cancels the running job and starts the stage over. The new restart tests cover only baseline, initial and rebase, leaving this requested behavior untested.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching targeted job, and add a restart test that verifies the same job completes and its command runs once.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a regression-retry-targeted check at the same SHA; the resumed stage cancels that job instead of attaching to it.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29-30 checks `pending.purpose === purpose` and `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`. The targeted retry purpose is `"regression-retry-targeted"` at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595, whereas resumed stage entry requests `"initial"` at line 1536. Rejection calls `await cancelGateExecution(...)` at src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:36 and clears the handle at line 42.
verification.trigger: Restart while an executor runs a targeted regression retry at the same SHA. The purpose mismatch cancels the surviving job, and the resumed stage starts initial gates again.

findings.title: Executor liveness has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined only by whether the recorded PID and birth time still match. The executor table has no heartbeat timestamp, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. New jobs are sent to it until pickup timeout, and waitStopped can wait indefinitely for a stalled owner after cancellation. The tests cover a dead PID and a release mismatch but never a live executor whose heartbeat stops.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and test a live but unresponsive executor for both fallback and cancellation behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops servicing jobs; the daemon treats it as fresh and a cancellation can remain blocked waiting for its acknowledgement.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354–359 selects executor rows and validates release and `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`, with no heartbeat timestamp. src/gates/lan.ts:102–105 cancellation calls `workers.cancel(handle.id)` then awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id)`. src/db/workers.ts:370–384 keeps waiting while that process identity exists.
verification.trigger: The executor event loop stalls while its process remains alive. It continues to qualify as available, and cancellation cannot finish because the executor never acknowledges shutdown.

findings.title: Pickup timeout test does not exercise in-process fallback
findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that sweep marks an unclaimed job failed. It never attaches through the gate executor or verifies that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that leaves an in-place job unclaimed, advances through pickup expiry, and asserts the local check executes and its GateRun is returned.
findings.failure_scenario: The sweep marks the job failed, but the attach loop fails to launch or return the in-process fallback; the existing test still passes.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–323 only enqueues, sweeps and asserts: `later.sweep(); expect(later.job(missed)?.state).toBe("failed"); expect(later.job(missed)?.attempt).toBe(1);`. It never attaches or awaits a GateRun. The fallback occurs separately at src/gates/lan.ts:130–139: `if (job.state === "failed")` followed by `await workers.waitStopped(...)` and `await local.start(request, controller.signal)`.
verification.trigger: An unpicked in-place job times out, but attaching to that failed job hangs or fails to return the local result. The pickup-timeout test still passes because it checks only database state.

findings.title: Executor tests replace the confinement they need to verify
findings.detail: The subprocess explicitly installs a no-op confinement wrapper, and the parent uses fakeConfinement. Consequently the test can pass even if executor gates run without the daemon's required confinement. Existing output and environment assertions do not exercise this boundary.
findings.suggestion: Add a platform-gated real confinement probe through the executor that checks both an allowed worktree operation and a denied out-of-scope write.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor launches a gate without its required confinement; every new executor test still passes because the test fixture disables confinement.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:86 wraps the executor in `confinementScope.run({ verify: async () => {}, wrap: cmd => cmd }, ... runInplaceExecutor(...))`. src/gates/inplace.ts:28 selects `confinementScope.getStore() ?? seatbeltForPort(cfg.port)`, so the fixture replaces real confinement with the no-op backend. test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:101 also wraps the daemon-side callback in `confinementScope.run(fakeConfinement, ...)`.
verification.trigger: The executor's confinement wiring regresses and gates execute without the required restrictions. These tests cannot detect the missing restrictions because their shared fixture deliberately runs commands without confinement and includes no denial probe.

findings.title: Executor output is redacted with an incomplete credential registry
findings.detail: Credential registration is process-local. The executor loads configuration, but it does not register credentials acquired by the daemon at runtime, such as its API token, GitHub token, or worker tokens. Gate output is redacted and truncated in the executor and then written to job events and results using that executor's registry. A credential known only to the daemon can therefore be persisted unredacted, and truncation can prevent the daemon from recognizing it later.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor's redaction policy cover the daemon's dynamically registered credentials before it captures, truncates, or persists gate output.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a daemon-registered API or GitHub token that is absent from the executor's credential registry; the token appears in the stored gate event or result.

verification.evidence: src/server/api-token.ts:9–10 creates a random token and calls `registerCredential("LIMITLESS_API_TOKEN", token)` in the daemon. src/cli/main.ts:426 starts the executor with `runInplaceExecutor(loadConfig(), sha, controller.signal)`; src/config.ts:264–267 registers configured provider credentials only. src/util/proc.ts:1216–1217 keeps credentials in process-local sets. src/gates/inplace.ts:65,69 writes check events and completion through WorkerStore; src/db/workers.ts:612–613 stores `this.sanitize(event)`, whose privacy filter uses `registeredCredentials()` from the current process (src/util/private-output.ts:11).
verification.trigger: A gate prints a token registered only in the daemon, absent from both the executor's registry and private-string policy. The executor's sanitization leaves it intact and persists it in gate_jobs events or results before daemon-side redaction can apply.

findings.title: A live but stalled executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only the PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor process remains alive but stops polling or renewing, the daemon continues to consider it available. For a leased job, waitStopped also waits indefinitely for that same process instead of reaching a confirmed-stop recovery path.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for a stale owner.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process stalls while running a gate and remains alive. Its lease expires, but the daemon waits indefinitely for stopped to become 1 and cannot fall back or start the next gate.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 fails an expired in-place lease. src/gates/lan.ts:130–131 then awaits `workers.waitStopped(...)`. src/db/workers.ts:366–384 waits on `stopped === 0` without a deadline and skips recovery while `this.executor(worker, false)` finds the live process.
verification.trigger: A stalled executor remains alive after its gate lease expires. The job becomes failed, but stopped remains zero, indefinitely blocking fallback or a subsequent gate in that worktree.

findings.title: Worktree exclusivity check races with job creation
findings.detail: The scan for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations with awaits between them. Two concurrent starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue distinct jobs, which separate executor processes can lease simultaneously. This defeats the required one-job-per-worktree guarantee.
findings.suggestion: Serialize reservation and enqueue for a worktree with an atomic database constraint or transaction, retaining the reservation until process cleanup is confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: Two gate starts for the same cwd run concurrently while two executors are available. Both pass the empty-job scan, enqueue, and execute checks in the same worktree at once.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54–59 scans existing jobs and waits for them before creating a handle. src/gates/lan.ts:72 then yields at `await releaseGateSlotScope()`. Enqueue happens later, in attach: `workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true)` (src/gates/lan.ts:80–81). Leasing only guards the individual row: `WHERE id=? AND state='queued'` (src/db/workers.ts:400), with no cwd exclusion.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both scan before either attaches. Both subsequently enqueue distinct jobs; two executors can lease them and run checks concurrently in the same worktree, violating worktree exclusivity.

findings.title: Restart discards running retry jobs
findings.detail: The request says that a resumed stage whose handle matches its stage, round, purpose, and SHA attaches to it, and explicitly includes the targeted retry. This allowlist rejects timeout and regression retry purposes even when all of those fields match. The stage’s initial resume check also cancels a recorded retry before it can be attached.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the recorded retry, and validate its matching handle without restricting resumption to the first execution.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor runs `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage cancels that job and repeats earlier gates instead of receiving the retry result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes with `"initial"`, then line 1547 executes initial gates. Targeted retries instead save purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"` through line 1595 and src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:86. The matching conditions at src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29-30 reject that purpose, and lines 35-43 cancel the job and clear its durable handle.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts during an in-place targeted regression retry. Stage replay discards the running retry and repeats earlier gate work rather than attaching to its result.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness
findings.detail: The request requires a fresh executor heartbeat and says the sweep applies freshness timers against it. Executor records contain only process identity and release, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. After a leased job expires, `waitStopped` also waits indefinitely while that process remains alive, preventing fallback.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a safe way to confirm its job processes have stopped when the executor stops responding.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops responding while a gate is running. The lease expires, yet the daemon waits indefinitely for `stopped=1` rather than completing the gate or safely failing over.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 defines executor liveness as `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. src/db/workers.ts:365–384 waits indefinitely for stopped while that identity remains present. src/gates/inplace.ts:80 sets `stopped=1` in the executor's finally block; a stalled event loop cannot reach it. src/gates/lan.ts:131 waits before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor stops responding during a gate without exiting. Lease expiry fails the job, but the daemon cannot complete fallback because the live executor never records stopped=1.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local repositories
findings.detail: The request says that when the executor is enabled and alive, the daemon’s local gate path creates an in-place job. With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor’s local fallback through the enabled in-place executor while retaining LAN dispatch for configured repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator uses LAN gates for one repository and enables the local executor; a different repository’s local gate still runs in the daemon and is lost on restart.

verification.evidence: src/app.ts:186 passes `cfg.executorEnabled` into `gateExecutorFor`. However, src/gates/executor.ts:79–81 handles LAN configuration with `case "lan": ... return lanExecutor(workers, repos);`, omitting the in-place flag. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults `inplace = false`, and line 71 routes unlisted repositories directly to `local.start(req, signal)`: `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`. That executor runs `runLocalGates` in the daemon (src/gates/executor.ts:130–139).
verification.trigger: Configure LAN gates for repository A, enable the in-place executor with a fresh matching-release heartbeat, then run gates for repository B outside workers.repos. B runs in the daemon instead of creating an in-place job, so a daemon restart interrupts its gates and requires rerunning them.

findings.title: Resume accepts jobs without a held lease
findings.detail: The request states, “A job is only re-attached while the executor still holds its lease.” `canResume` also accepts queued jobs and completed jobs without checking a held lease. This deviates from the requested restart boundary.
findings.suggestion: Require a current executor-held lease for reattachment, or explicitly define and implement a separate completed-result recovery rule.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after saving a handle while the job is still queued; the resumed stage reattaches to that unleased job instead of starting fresh.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:35–40 explicitly accepts an unleased queued job: `j.state === "queued" ? !!workers.executor() : j.state === "leased" && ... (j.lease_expires_at ?? 0) > workers.now()`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:33 uses `executor?.canResume?.(pending.handle, env)` to accept a matching recorded in-place handle.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts with a saved matching handle whose job remains queued, while a same-release executor is alive. Resume accepts and attaches to that job despite no executor holding its lease, contrary to the required lease prerequisite.

candidates.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. A daemon from before this change never updates that setting, so after rollback it still contains the newer release SHA. The newer executor continues its running job while the older daemon resumes the run without understanding the in-place handle, allowing both releases to operate on the same worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
candidates.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

candidates.detail: The request says that when the executor is enabled and alive, the daemon’s local gate path creates an in-place job. With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.
candidates.suggestion: Route the LAN executor’s local fallback through the enabled in-place executor while retaining LAN dispatch for configured repositories.
candidates.failure_scenario: A coordinator uses LAN gates for one repository and enables the local executor; a different repository’s local gate still runs in the daemon and is lost on restart.

candidates.title: Resume accepts jobs without a held lease
candidates.detail: The request states, “A job is only re-attached while the executor still holds its lease.” `canResume` also accepts queued jobs and completed jobs without checking a held lease. This deviates from the requested restart boundary.
candidates.suggestion: Require a current executor-held lease for reattachment, or explicitly define and implement a separate completed-result recovery rule.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after saving a handle while the job is still queued; the resumed stage reattaches to that unleased job instead of starting fresh.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required owner and mode
findings.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. It does not check the file's owner, and it accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite requiring mode 0600. A file owned by another user can therefore pass the metadata check even when the daemon cannot read it, deferring failure until a configured repository first needs a token.
findings.suggestion: Check the file owner and enforce the requested mode and readability during configuration loading, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A key file owned by another user has mode 0600. Its metadata passes this check, but the daemon cannot read it and App-authenticated GitHub calls fail later.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 calls only `statSync(privateKeyPath)`; src/config.ts:394 checks `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`, without checking ownership or actual readability. src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64 reads the key later; lines 66–67 report `cannot read or sign with private key`.
verification.trigger: A different user's mode-0600 key has accessible metadata but is unreadable by the daemon: configuration succeeds and App GitHub operations subsequently fail.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. A key placed in a repository checkout or another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate despite the requirement that the key never reach them.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the key to a protected location or add its canonical path to every agent and gate read-deny policy, including aliases.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator configures `private_key_path` to a mode-0600 file in a checkout. An agent running as the same user can read that file through its permitted checkout access.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:387 uses `resolve(configDir, a.private_key_path)` without restricting the resulting location. src/harness/read-policy.ts:42 sets `denyRead` to `[...paths("deny_read"), configDir]`, without adding the App key. src/harness/codex.ts:321–324 grants `/` read access and checkout write access, then applies configured denies.
verification.trigger: Configure a mode-0600 key inside an agent-accessible checkout outside the config directory and existing denied paths: startup accepts it, and the same-user agent can read the App private key.

findings.title: Key validation does not verify the file owner or required mode
findings.detail: The check accepts any owner-readable file with no group or world permission, including mode 0400 or 0700, and never checks its UID. It therefore does not enforce the requested owner-owned, mode-0600 key file; in particular, a file owned by another account can pass validation where the daemon has elevated access.
findings.suggestion: Check the file's owner against the daemon's effective UID and enforce the requested permission bits, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A regular key file owned by a different UID with mode 0600 is readable by an elevated daemon; startup accepts it even though the daemon does not own the file.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:394 checks file type and permission bits but never `key.uid`; src/config.ts:409 accepts the resulting `privateKeyPath`. A different-owner mode-0600 file therefore passes. However, the request specifies readability only by the file's owner, without explicitly requiring its UID to match an elevated daemon's UID.
verification.trigger: An elevated daemon accepts a mode-0600 key belonging to another UID. This violates the claimed ownership policy if daemon ownership is required; the requirement's ownership wording leaves that interpretation uncertain.

findings.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
findings.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App without fallback. The manual landing script invokes this checker for its merge, but the checker calls sh directly and never loads or configures the identity provider. Its merge therefore uses the owner's gh login even when the repository is configured for the App; its PR reads and the direct gh calls in land-pr.sh have the same gap.
findings.suggestion: Load the configured identity in the manual landing path and route its repository-scoped gh calls through the shared provider, including the calls made directly by land-pr.sh.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator runs scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: the PR is merged as the owner, and an App token exchange failure cannot stop that merge.

verification.evidence: scripts/land-pr.sh:153 invokes `check_private "$pr" "$repo" --merge "$sha"`. scripts/check-private-strings.ts:55–56 builds `const merge = ["gh", "pr", "merge", pr, "-R", repo, "--squash", "--delete-branch"]` and executes `await sh([...merge, "--subject", title, "--body", data.body, "--match-head-commit", sha], opts)`. This script never loads or configures the App identity. App-token injection occurs in src/integrations/github-identity.ts:121–125 through `await githubIdentity(repo)` and `GH_TOKEN: identity.token`, which this direct `sh` call bypasses.
verification.trigger: Run scripts/land-pr.sh for its repository when that repository is configured to use the App, with the owner's gh login active and no overriding token. After checks pass, the script merges as the owner without attempting an App token exchange; an exchange failure therefore cannot block the merge.

findings.title: Token exchange ignores caller cancellation and timeout
findings.detail: The provider creates its own 30-second timeout and does not accept the caller's abort signal or deadline. A GitHub operation can therefore remain in the shared token exchange after its caller is cancelled, and the initial token request plus the App lookup can each consume 30 seconds before the requested gh command starts.
findings.suggestion: Propagate cancellation and the operation's deadline through identity acquisition, while preserving safe handling of concurrent callers sharing an exchange.
findings.failure_scenario: A run is cancelled while its first installation-token request is stalled. The run continues waiting for the provider's timeout instead of ending promptly.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/github-identity.ts:121 awaits `githubIdentity(repo)` before calling `sh` with `opts`. The provider accepts only `repo` (line 54), and its fetch uses `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` (line 26). Neither the caller's signal nor its timeout reaches token acquisition.
verification.trigger: An App repository has no cached token and its exchange stalls. Cancelling the caller does not interrupt its await; it remains pending until the exchange completes or the provider's 30-second timeout fires. The caller's command timeout also starts only after identity acquisition.

Verifier: 7 candidates, 7 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: New worker reports are rejected by older coordinators
findings.detail: The result schema was strict in the previous release. A new worker includes failureClass in an authentication failure report, so an older coordinator rejects the report as containing an unknown field. This breaks mixed-version operation and can leave the job failing instead of falling back locally.
findings.suggestion: Make protocol evolution compatible with older coordinators, for example through capability negotiation or a staged release that first permits unknown result fields.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker is upgraded before its coordinator and reports a Claude authentication failure with failureClass set; the older coordinator's strict AgentResultReport validation rejects it.

verification.evidence: HEAD src/workers/agent-protocol.ts:31 adds `failureClass: z.literal("authentication").optional()`. src/workers/client.ts:912-925 builds and sends a report containing `...result`. At base c3e4786, src/workers/agent-protocol.ts:28-82 omits failureClass and ends AgentResultReport with `.strict()`. src/server/workers.ts:249 validates incoming reports with `AgentResultReport.parse(body)`; lines 313-316 return HTTP 400 on validation failure.
verification.trigger: Upgrade a worker before its coordinator; a Claude authentication failure produces a report containing failureClass="authentication". The older coordinator rejects that report as an unknown field with HTTP 400.

findings.title: Authentication fallback can follow adoption of a partial worker commit
findings.detail: Authentication errors can occur after earlier model turns and tool calls, but the parser classifies them identically to a login rejection before the session. The worker publishes any changes before reporting the result, and this path adopts that commit before falling back locally. Consequently the local implementer runs on top of partial work from the failed session, and that work is already published even if the local invocation also fails.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a rejection before any session work from an authentication failure after work began, and handle partial work without treating the session as one that never ran.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker implementer edits files during an initial successful turn, then its token expires on a later API call. The worker publishes the edits, the coordinator adopts them, and an authentication fallback starts a local implementer against that partial commit.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:905 calls `publishAgentChanges(...)` after the harness result without excluding authentication failures. src/harness/claude.ts:478 classifies `parser.authenticationFailed` without requiring zero turns. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:201 executes `await publication?.adopt(sha, request as AgentPublication)` before checking `result.failureClass !== "authentication"` at line 211 and calling `return fallback(id)` at line 217.
verification.trigger: A worker makes edits, then receives a structured authentication failure on a later API call. Its partial changes are published and adopted before the local fallback starts, so the local implementer runs against that partial worker commit.

findings.title: Treating every authentication error as a startup failure can replay completed work
findings.detail: The parser marks an authentication error regardless of whether the session has already made successful model calls or executed tools. The LAN executor then adopts the worker commit and runs the same round locally, while coordinator routing can also start another candidate. A token that expires during a multi-turn session can therefore cause completed edits or other tool side effects to be repeated, even though the worker did run the session.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish an authentication rejection before any session work from one after successful turns or tool calls, and only use the startup fallback for the former.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker edits files in a successful first turn, then receives a 401 on a later API call. Its commit is adopted and the implement prompt is run again locally against that changed checkout.

verification.evidence: src/harness/claude.ts:146 sets `this.authenticationFailed = this.isError && (this.authenticationFailed || e.api_error_status === 401)` without checking prior tool activity. src/workers/client.ts:905 calls `publishAgentChanges(...)` after the failed session. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:201 calls `await publication?.adopt(sha, request as AgentPublication)` before lines 208–217 send authentication failures to `return fallback(id)`. Line 57 defines fallback as `local()`.
verification.trigger: A worker edits files before a later API request returns an authentication error. The worker publishes those edits, the coordinator adopts them, and then repeats the implementation prompt locally against the changed checkout.

findings.title: Authentication retry events are ignored when the CLI times out before its final result
findings.detail: The captured stream contains structured system api_retry events with error_status 401 and error authentication_failed, but the parser ignores them. If the invocation deadline or idle timeout expires while Claude is retrying, runClaude returns timeout or stuck without an authentication failure class. Context.invoke does not fall back on those statuses, so an implement stage can again proceed as a finished round after no implementer authenticated.
findings.suggestion: Track structured authentication rejection in retry events and preserve that classification when the process ends before the final result, while retaining cancellation semantics.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude emits the fixture's 401 api_retry events but its retries exceed the invocation deadline before the assistant and result events arrive; the harness returns timeout and the pipeline proceeds with the failed implementation.

verification.evidence: test/fixtures/claude-authentication.jsonl:2 contains `"subtype":"api_retry"` with `"error_status":401` and `"error":"authentication_failed"`. src/harness/claude.ts:85–90 handles system events only when `e.subtype === "init"`. Line 475 returns `status: "timeout"` before the authentication classification at line 478. src/pipeline/context.ts:1177 returns the task result, and src/pipeline/engine.ts:1396–1403 records its issue and saves `"implementation-ready"`; line 1422 sets `implementedRound = round`.
verification.trigger: The stream emits structured authentication retry events, but the invocation deadline expires before its assistant/result events. The harness returns timeout without the authentication failure class, so implementation proceeds as a completed round instead of falling back for authentication.

findings.title: Distinguish startup authentication failures from failures after agent work
findings.detail: Any terminal 401 is classified as a failure before the session could run, even if earlier turns successfully called tools and changed files. The coordinator then starts another candidate for the same invocation; on a worker, the coordinator can first adopt the worker's commit and then run the round locally. This can repeat work and side effects and contradicts the meaning of the new failure class.
findings.suggestion: Track whether the session has performed agent work and only use the startup authentication fallback when the structured failure establishes that no work ran. Handle a later authentication failure as an interrupted session with its existing work preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: A tool-enabled Claude session edits files successfully, then its token expires before a subsequent API request. The final result has `is_error: true` and `api_error_status: 401`, so it is classified as an authentication startup failure and another agent is invoked on the partially completed work.

verification.evidence: src/harness/claude.ts:93 unconditionally sets `authenticationFailed` for `e.error === "authentication_failed"`; line 146 also accepts an error result with `api_error_status === 401`. Lines 478–483 return `status: "unavailable", failureClass: "authentication"` without checking turns or tool activity. src/pipeline/context.ts:1112–1122 handles that class by recording the provider failure and executing `continue`, invoking another candidate.
verification.trigger: A tool-enabled session modifies files and then receives a 401 on a subsequent request. Its partial work remains, but the invocation is treated like an authentication startup failure and another candidate receives the same task against that work.

findings.title: Authentication failures can exhaust routing before an available candidate is tried
findings.detail: The request says authentication failure makes the provider unavailable for this invocation and that the invocation falls back to the next candidate. Unlike the confinement failure branch immediately above it, this branch consumes one of the unpinned routing loop’s six attempts. Six authentication failures therefore end the invocation even when another configured provider can run it.
findings.suggestion: Exclude authentication failures from the attempt budget, as confinement failures are excluded, while retaining the per-provider exclusion that prevents retries.
findings.failure_scenario: An unpinned invocation has seven eligible providers. The first six return structured authentication failures and the seventh would succeed; the loop exits after the sixth and sends the run to needs_human without trying the seventh.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/context.ts:612 limits unpinned routing to `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < (chain ? Infinity : 6); attempt++)`. The authentication branch records the provider and executes `continue` without decrementing `attempt` (src/pipeline/context.ts:1112–1122). After six failures, src/pipeline/context.ts:1180–1183 throws `new NoCapacityError(...` with `Gave up routing`, without checking remaining candidates.
verification.trigger: An unpinned invocation has seven eligible providers and sufficient time remaining. The first six return structured authentication failures; each consumes a routing attempt, so the seventh provider is never tried even though it would succeed.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips it when `!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2009–2013 updates and publishes the run without recording a lifecycle effect.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between polls. No pending lifecycle event exists, so the required needs-you comment and reason are lost.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines eligibility as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 executes `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue`. src/integrations/index.ts:66–67 starts the lifecycle-owning queue only when queue repositories and trusted accounts are configured.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #42 in a GitHub-integrated repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Lifecycle reconciliation skips the issue entirely.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
findings.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.

findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes only interruption points: `test.each(["after label", "after comment"])`; its assertions explicitly check `"comment:started"` (1291, 1298) and `"limitless:in-progress"` (1295). findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments

findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:134-137 calls 'redactCredentials' directly on the comment body; lines 140-148 check only loadPrivateStrings entries before line 163 posts it. src/util/proc.ts:1234-1236 registers literal, newline-normalized and JSON-escaped credential variants, without percent-encoded variants. src/gates/private.ts:193-196 matches decoded layers only against configured entries.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs the predictable marker '<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->'. Lines 159-164 save the effect as 'pending' before POST; lines 128-130 accept any comment containing the marker and save 'done'.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })`. Lines 128-130 accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then `save(effect, "done")` and skip posting; no author identity is checked.
verification.trigger: A lifecycle comment remains pending after an unsuccessful POST or restart. Another participant posts its predictable marker. Reconciliation accepts that comment as the factory's completed write and suppresses the notification.

findings.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority-label event, even if that label has since been removed. The separately computed `approved` set can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so a withdrawn re-approval still permits the issue to run.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. A trusted account applies `priority:1` after failure and subsequently removes it to withdraw approval. The old `priority:2` satisfies `approved`, while the historical `priority:1` event satisfies this check, so the failed issue is picked again.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:61-63 collects all priority `LabeledEvent` entries. :99 accepts any trusted entry later than `failedAt`, whereas :74-81 independently accepts the remaining pre-failure priority label. Neither check requires the post-failure label to remain applied.
verification.trigger: An issue retains trusted priority:2 from before failure; trusted priority:1 is applied afterward and removed to withdraw approval. Both independent checks pass, permitting another pickup.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to repositories in the issue queue
findings.detail: The request covers “any start path,” but reconciliation skips every repository outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run against another repository therefore receives none of the required lifecycle labels or comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #12` for a repository that is not configured in `githubQueue.repos`; no in-progress label or lifecycle comments are posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:43 contains `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`; lines 10-12 require membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1580-1592 explicitly tests outside-repository and disabled configurations and expects no labels or comments.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #12 targets a repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Its issue receives no lifecycle labels or comments. This duplicates C13.

findings.title: Transitions occurring between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The requirement says each lifecycle event is a durable side effect and must not lose a label change or comment across restarts. The reconciler derives needs-human, failed, and cancelled events solely from the current run status; it creates no pending effect when the transition occurs. If the run advances again before the next poll, that event is permanently invisible.
findings.suggestion: Durably enqueue lifecycle effects at the state transition and reconcile those recorded effects on each poll.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll, or the daemon restarts and the run is resumed before reconciliation. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 creates the needs_human event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless their effect is already pending. src/db/store.ts:2037-2040 permits needs_human to become resolved, while src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:18-25 derives labels solely from current status.
verification.trigger: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before reconciliation first observes it, including across a restart. No pending notification exists, so the needs-you label and reason comment are omitted. Retry creates a separate run (src/app.ts:431-434), but resolution proves the claimed loss of intervening transitions.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The request requires a trusted priority application after the failure label. This check accepts any historical trusted priority event after failure, even if that priority label was subsequently removed. A different priority label that was already present before the failure can then supply `approved`, so the issue is picked without a currently applied post-failure approval.
findings.suggestion: Require the post-failure trusted event to be the latest application of a currently present, approved priority label.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue has trusted `priority:2` before failure; afterward a trusted account briefly applies and removes `priority:3`. The remaining pre-failure `priority:2` makes the issue eligible.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:99 uses `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)` without checking current label membership. :74-81 allows the existing priority:2 label to supply approval; :129 omits removal events from the timeline query.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:2 remains from before failure, and a trusted account briefly applies then removes priority:3 afterward. The removed priority:3 event satisfies re-approval, allowing the issue to be picked again.

candidates.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
candidates.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile each recorded occurrence independently.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-configured repositories
candidates.detail: The reconciler skips every repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos or has no trusted queue accounts, and it is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The requested lifecycle applies to runs started through every entry point; it is not limited to repositories enabled for automatic issue picking.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for linked issues.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that has no issue queue configured. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be re-picked
candidates.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed, and a write failure is caught before the queue continues to query candidates. The queue's latestIssueRun lookup only recognizes issue source references, so a terminal CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` supplies no local re-approval guard.
candidates.suggestion: Make admission account for terminal runs linked through all supported start paths, including while lifecycle writes are pending.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

candidates.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
candidates.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
candidates.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
candidates.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation skips every repository absent from githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler itself is started only when the queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts. candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle label or comment is posted.

candidates.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
candidates.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.

candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

candidates.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered
candidates.detail: Comment checkpoints are keyed only by run and event name. Once a needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot post its new reason. Label reconciliation can still switch back to needs-you, leaving the issue with a stale explanation.
candidates.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status episode rather than only by event type.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

candidates.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

candidates.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

candidates.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
candidates.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.

candidates.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

candidates.suggestion: Create and check a fixed fallback body and keep its delivery pending until it is posted; test that the fallback is posted once.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link or run identifier; the issue receives no lifecycle comment and no later poll retries it.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: Both terminal comments contain only a status and UI link. The request requires a comment with the reason, and the tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent. Readers cannot tell from the issue why the run failed or what needs attention.
candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using a fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human with an actionable question or fails with an error; the issue receives only “needs you: see …” or “failed: see …”.

candidates.title: Blocked publication text permanently suppresses the comment
candidates.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed message. The same happens when a pending body fails its check before delivery. This permanently loses the lifecycle notification rather than providing the safe fallback required by the request.
candidates.suggestion: Prepare and publish a fixed, checked fallback message when the original text is blocked, and retain the effect as pending until delivery succeeds.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or run ID contains a private string. The label is updated, but no lifecycle comment is ever posted, including after subsequent polls or restarts.

candidates.title: Lifecycle writes are restricted to repositories enabled for the issue queue
candidates.detail: Reconciliation accepts only repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts, and the only caller is the queue poller, which does not start without that configuration. Runs started directly, through MCP, or through GitHub triggers for other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments, although the request covers any start path.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues for all supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured repository has no issue queue enabled and an owner starts `limitless run` with `Closes #123`; issue 123 never receives the in-progress label or lifecycle comments.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The request requires updates for “any start path,” but lifecycleManaged requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured. The reconciler itself is started only when the issue queue is enabled. CLI, MCP, and trigger runs against other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include every linked issue from the supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts a CLI run with Closes #42 in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Blocked publication text silently discards the comment
candidates.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” Instead, a publication check failure marks the effect done without posting anything. The same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check.
candidates.suggestion: Checkpoint and deliver a fixed, safe fallback comment when the original body is blocked.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or another generated comment field contains a private string; the check rejects the body and the lifecycle comment is permanently skipped.

candidates.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: When the latest run failed but the failed label is absent, admission falls back to accepting a trusted priority event after the run's finish time. If the failure-label write is delayed or fails, this permits re-pick before the required failure label and subsequent approval exist.
candidates.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence that its failure label was applied and that a trusted priority application followed that label.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails, its GitHub label write fails, and a trusted user reapplies a priority label before the next poll. The next admission check can start another run without any priority application after the failure label.

findings.title: Transitions between polls can be lost

If a run reaches needs_human or failed and then changes status before the next poll, there is no recorded event to reconcile, so its label and comment are never delivered. The tests change status and poll before changing it again; they do not cover an unobserved intermediate transition.

Lifecycle reconciliation does not consume transition history.
